title: Three Right Answers to One Probability Question
hook: Pick a 'random' chord of a circle: is it longer than a side of the inscribed equilateral triangle? Three perfectly reasonable methods give 1/3, 1/2 and 1/4, and none of them is wrong.
core_insight: A probability is not defined until the sample space and the sampling procedure are defined; 'at random' is a modeling choice, not a fact of nature.
key_visual: One circle, three samplers running side by side: (a) two random endpoints on the rim, (b) a random point along a random radius, (c) a random midpoint inside the disk. Chords rain down in each panel, gold if longer than the triangle side, and running tallies converge to 1/3, 1/2 and 1/4. Then each method's chord midpoints are shown as a heat map: three visibly different densities explain the three answers.
build_fail_iterate: Code 'random chord' three natural ways and expect agreement; the simulations stubbornly disagree. Diagnose by plotting where each method puts chord midpoints. Finish with Jaynes's fix: demand that the answer not change when the circle is rotated, scaled or shifted, which singles out the 1/2 method for a specific physical setup (straws tossed onto a circle).
real_world_anchor: Joseph Bertrand, Calcul des probabilites (1889); E. T. Jaynes, 'The Well-Posed Problem', Foundations of Physics (1973), which argued for 1/2 via invariance for a concrete physical process.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Do not present 1/2 as the universally correct answer; Jaynes's argument applies to a particular physical process. State exactly what is uniform in each method (endpoints on the rim, distance from the center, midpoint area).

title: When a 99% Accurate Test Says You're Sick
hook: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people, and a test catches 99% of cases with a 1% false-positive rate. If you test positive, the chance you actually have the disease is about 9%.
core_insight: Bayes' theorem is just shrinking the sample space to the outcomes consistent with the evidence; when a condition is rare, false positives from the huge healthy group swamp the true positives.
key_visual: A 100 x 100 grid of 10,000 dots, 10 of them 'sick'. A test beam sweeps across: about 10 sick dots light red and about 100 healthy dots light orange. Everything unlit fades away, leaving the new, smaller sample space where red is visibly a small minority (about 9%). A second independent test is applied only to the lit dots and the red share jumps to about 91%.
build_fail_iterate: Naive approach: read '99% accurate' as P(sick | positive) = 99%. Simulate 10,000 people and count: the naive answer is off by a factor of about 11. Fix: switch to natural frequencies (counts of people, not percentages), then show the same calculation as Bayes' rule drawn with rectangles.
real_world_anchor: Gigerenzer et al. (2007), 'Helping Doctors and Patients Make Sense of Health Statistics', Psychological Science in the Public Interest: in a training session only 21% of 160 gynecologists chose the correct answer (about 1 in 10) to a mammography screening problem; natural-frequency formats greatly improved performance.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: 'Accuracy' alone is ambiguous: state sensitivity, specificity (or false-positive rate) and prevalence separately. The 9% assumes the person was tested at random from the population; symptoms or risk factors raise the prior and change the answer.

title: Randomness Looks Clumpier Than You Think
hook: During the 1944 flying-bomb attacks on London, many people believed the bombs were targeting particular neighborhoods because the hits seemed to cluster. A statistician showed the clusters were just what pure chance predicts.
core_insight: Truly random (Poisson) events produce clusters and gaps; evenly spread patterns are the real sign of non-randomness. Our intuition for 'random' is too uniform.
key_visual: Two panels, each with 537 dots on a 24 x 24 grid of squares: one truly uniform-random, one 'human random' (a jittered grid). The viewer guesses which is random. Then each square is shaded by its hit count and a histogram of counts builds bar by bar beside the Poisson curve (lambda = 537/576, about 0.93), landing on Clarke's actual table.
build_fail_iterate: Build a 'target detector' that flags any square with 3 or more hits as deliberately targeted; on pure noise it flags dozens. Fix: compare the whole distribution of counts to the Poisson null instead of eyeballing hotspots. Then plant a few genuinely aimed squares and show what real targeting does to the histogram's tail.
real_world_anchor: R. D. Clarke (1946), 'An Application of the Poisson Distribution', Journal of the Institute of Actuaries: 537 flying-bomb hits over 576 quarter-square-kilometre areas of south London; observed counts of 229, 211, 93, 35, 7 and 1 squares with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5+ hits closely matched Poisson expectations.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Clarke tested for clustering within the studied area at that scale; it does not show the bombs were unaimed (they were aimed at London, just imprecisely). These were V-1 flying bombs, not V-2 rockets.

title: The Hidden Bias That Hid the Hot Hand
hook: Flip a fair coin four times and record the fraction of heads that immediately follow a heads. Averaged over all possible sequences, that fraction is not 50%; it is about 40.5%.
core_insight: Selecting the flips that follow a streak inside a finite sequence creates a subtle selection bias. Correcting for it overturned a famous conclusion that the basketball 'hot hand' is a pure illusion.
key_visual: All 16 four-flip sequences laid out as rows of coins. In each row the flips that follow an H are highlighted and the share that are also H is written at the right; TTTT and TTTH gray out as undefined. The 14 proportions drop onto a number line and their average settles at 17/42, about 0.405, well left of 0.5.
build_fail_iterate: Write the 'obvious' streak test (compare P(hit | previous hit) with P(hit) within each shooter's sequence) and run it on a simulated shooter who is perfectly random: it reports a 'cold hand'. Fix: compute the expected bias under the null by permuting each sequence, then re-test against that corrected baseline.
real_world_anchor: Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky (1985), Cognitive Psychology, concluded the hot hand was a cognitive illusion; Miller & Sanjurjo (2018), 'Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? A Truth in the Law of Small Numbers', Econometrica, identified the bias and, re-analysing GVT's Cornell shooting data, found evidence consistent with a hot hand.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Each individual flip is still 50/50; the bias comes from averaging per-sequence proportions, not from the coin having memory. The bias shrinks as sequences lengthen. Say 'evidence consistent with a modest hot hand', not 'proved the hot hand is real'; the debate continues.

title: Why Random Darts Beat Grids in 100 Dimensions
hook: To integrate a function in 20 dimensions with just 10 grid points per axis, you would need 10^20 evaluations. Random sampling gets a usable answer with thousands, and its error shrinks at the same rate in any dimension.
core_insight: Monte Carlo error falls like 1/sqrt(N) whatever the dimension (with a constant set by the variance), while grid methods suffer exponentially as dimension grows: randomness is a computational tool, not just noise.
key_visual: Darts fall on a square containing a quarter circle; the gold fraction ticks toward pi/4 and a pi readout converges. Then the grid alternative explodes: 10 points on a line, 100 on a square, 1,000 in a cube, and a counter racing to 10^20 as dimensions climb. Overlaid log-log error curves show Monte Carlo's slope of -1/2 staying fixed as d grows while the grid's convergence lines flatten.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: estimate the volume of a 10-D ball with a grid; the point count explodes. Switch to darts in the surrounding cube: fine at 10-D, but at 30-D essentially no darts land inside the ball (it fills about 2e-14 of the cube), so the estimate is all zeros. Fix: importance sampling from a distribution concentrated where the ball is, and watch the variance collapse.
real_world_anchor: Metropolis & Ulam (1949), 'The Monte Carlo Method', Journal of the American Statistical Association; the idea grew from Stanislaw Ulam's 1946 musings on solitaire odds and neutron-diffusion work with John von Neumann at Los Alamos.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The 1/sqrt(N) rate is dimension-independent, but the variance constant can blow up with dimension (as the ball example shows); do not call Monte Carlo 'immune' to dimension. Pseudo-random numbers are fine for this purpose; true randomness is not required.

title: Seven Shuffles: When a Deck Suddenly Becomes Random
hook: Riffle-shuffle a deck four times and it is still far from random; a magician can exploit what is left. Around seven shuffles the deck becomes close to random, and the distance to randomness drops off a cliff rather than fading smoothly.
core_insight: A shuffle is a Markov chain on the 52! orderings of the deck; such chains can show a sharp 'cutoff' in mixing, so 'how many steps until random?' has a surprisingly crisp answer.
key_visual: The deck is drawn as a vertical rainbow (card 1 red through card 52 violet). Each riffle cuts and interleaves the bands; after 1 to 4 shuffles long rising color runs are still obvious, by 7 to 8 it is visual static. Beside it, total-variation distance to uniform is plotted per shuffle: 1.00, 1.00, 1.00, 1.00, 0.92, 0.61, 0.33, 0.17, a visible cliff.
build_fail_iterate: Naive randomness test: 'is the top card uniformly distributed?' It passes after a couple of shuffles and falsely declares victory. Better test: count rising sequences, which exposes the structure the top-card test misses. Then show the full distance curve under the Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model. Bonus failure: overhand shuffling, which needs orders of magnitude more shuffles.
real_world_anchor: Bayer & Diaconis (1992), 'Trailing the Dovetail Shuffle to Its Lair', Annals of Applied Probability, using the Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model of riffle shuffling.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: 'Seven' depends on the distance measure (total variation) and the GSR model; other criteria give different numbers (Trefethen & Trefethen, 2000, argued about six under an entropy measure). After seven shuffles the distance is about 0.33, i.e. 'reasonably close', not perfectly random.

title: How Much Information Is in a Letter?
hook: With 26 letters, each one should carry log2(26), about 4.7 bits. Shannon estimated that printed English carries only around one bit per letter: most of what you read is predictable.
core_insight: Information is surprise: entropy is the average number of yes/no questions needed to pin down an outcome, and it depends on the probabilities, not on how many outcomes are possible.
key_visual: A probability bar split into letter-colored segments is recursively bisected by yes/no questions, growing a binary tree whose average depth is the entropy. Then context is added: after 'Q' the bar collapses almost entirely onto 'U' and the tree shrinks to nearly nothing. A bits-per-letter meter falls from 4.7 (all letters equal) to about 4.1 (letter frequencies) to about 1 (long context).
build_fail_iterate: Build a naive compressor with fixed 5-bit codes per letter. Improve it with a Huffman code (short codes for E and T) and gain a little. Add context, predicting each letter from the previous ones, and watch the bit rate plunge toward Shannon's estimate. Show the floor: no code can beat the entropy on average.
real_world_anchor: Claude Shannon, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (1948) and 'Prediction and Entropy of Printed English' (1951), which used human guessing experiments to estimate roughly 0.6 to 1.3 bits per letter given long contexts.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Shannon's ~1 bit per letter is an estimated range from prediction experiments, not an exact constant; single-letter-frequency entropy is about 4.1 bits. Entropy measures unpredictability, not meaning or importance.

title: The Distance That Isn't Symmetric
hook: KL divergence is often called a 'distance' between probability distributions, yet the divergence from A to B can differ wildly from B to A. Which direction you minimize decides whether a model covers every possibility or confidently picks one.
core_insight: KL(P||Q) is the extra bits you pay for coding data from P with a code built for Q. Minimizing it over Q forces Q to cover all of P's mass (mode-covering); minimizing KL(Q||P) lets Q lock onto a single mode (mode-seeking).
key_visual: A two-humped target P in blue. A single Gaussian Q in orange is fitted live twice: under forward KL(P||Q) it stretches into a wide blob spanning both humps; under reverse KL(Q||P) it slides onto one hump and hugs it. The integrand is shaded beneath each, showing why 'Q near zero where P is not' is catastrophic in one direction but harmless in the other.
build_fail_iterate: Naively treat KL as a distance: compute it both ways on the same pair and get two different numbers. Then fit a one-hump model to two-hump data in each direction and watch the two qualitatively different failures. Connect forward KL to maximum likelihood (which minimizes KL from the data distribution) and reverse KL to the mode-seeking behaviour of variational inference.
real_world_anchor: Kullback & Leibler (1951), 'On Information and Sufficiency', Annals of Mathematical Statistics; the mode-covering versus mode-seeking contrast is the standard illustration in Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), Chapter 10.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: KL is non-negative and zero only when the distributions match, but it is asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality, so it is not a metric. State which argument plays the role of the 'true' distribution; conventions differ across fields.

title: Why Bell Curves Are Everywhere, and When They're Not
hook: Collecting more data does not make your data look more normal. What becomes normal is the average, and for some ordinary-looking distributions even the average never settles down.
core_insight: The Central Limit Theorem: sums and averages of many independent pieces with finite variance become approximately normal, whatever the pieces look like. With infinite variance (for example the Cauchy distribution) averaging does not tame the noise.
key_visual: A Galton board whose bins morph into a normal curve as rows of pegs are added. Then the source changes: dice, skewed exponential waiting times, lopsided coins; each time the histogram of sample means melts into the same bell and narrows like 1/sqrt(n). Finally a Cauchy source: the histogram of means refuses to narrow and occasional giant outliers jerk the running mean around.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: collect 10,000 skewed observations and expect the raw histogram to become normal; it stays skewed. Fix: plot means of samples instead. Then break it: switch to Cauchy draws (a ratio of two normals) and watch the running mean lurch forever. Diagnose infinite variance; fix with the median, which does converge.
real_world_anchor: Francis Galton's 'quincunx' (bean machine), described in Natural Inheritance (1889); early versions of the theorem by de Moivre (1733) and Laplace (1810).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The CLT needs independence (or weak dependence) and finite variance, and how large n must be depends on skewness; heavily skewed data can need far more than the folk rule of 30. Galton's board shows a binomial approaching a normal, a special case of the CLT.

title: Why the Best Schools Are Small, and So Are the Worst
hook: Rank schools by average test score and the smallest schools crowd the top of the list, an observation that helped fuel big investments in small schools. But the smallest schools also crowd the bottom.
core_insight: Averages from small groups vary more (the standard error scales like sigma/sqrt(n)), so the extremes of any ranking are dominated by small units; ranking rates without accounting for sample size mostly ranks noise.
key_visual: A funnel plot: each school is a dot with enrollment on x and mean score on y. Small schools spray wide, large ones hug the overall mean, and dashed control limits at plus/minus 2 sigma/sqrt(n) trace the funnel exactly. Then the same funnel reappears for county cancer rates on a stylized grid map, where both the 'healthiest' and 'deadliest' counties light up as the same sparsely populated ones.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: rank units by raw rate and copy the top ten. Simulate schools that are all identical and still 'discover' that small is better. Fix 1: funnel plot with control limits. Fix 2: shrink each school's mean toward the overall mean in proportion to its noise (empirical Bayes) and watch the small schools' extreme ranks evaporate.
real_world_anchor: Howard Wainer (2007), 'The Most Dangerous Equation', American Scientist, on de Moivre's equation, the small-schools movement (including Gates Foundation funding) and U.S. county kidney-cancer rates; see also Gelman & Nolan, Teaching Statistics: A Bag of Tricks (2002).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: This does not show small schools are better or worse, only that raw rankings cannot tell. Show both tails explicitly so viewers do not walk away with 'small schools are bad'.

title: How Serial Numbers Counted Germany's Tanks
hook: In World War II, Allied intelligence estimated German tank production at around 1,400 a month. Statisticians working only from serial numbers on captured equipment estimated about 250, and postwar German records showed they were almost exactly right.
core_insight: Maximum likelihood picks the parameter value that makes the observed data most probable, here the largest serial number seen. MLEs can be biased; a small correction (m + m/k - 1) fixes it by adding the average gap between observed numbers.
key_visual: A number line from 1 to an unknown N; k captured serial numbers drop as glowing ticks. The likelihood curve L(N) draws itself: zero below the largest tick, then decaying, so its peak sits exactly at the maximum. The average gap between ticks is measured and copied above the maximum. Thousands of simulated captures show the MLE's histogram sitting left of the truth while the corrected estimator centers on it.
build_fail_iterate: Naive 1: double the mean serial number; roughly unbiased but can produce an estimate below the largest observed number, which is absurd. Naive 2: use the maximum (the MLE); it always underestimates. Fix: m(1 + 1/k) - 1, the minimum-variance unbiased estimator. Compare all three sampling distributions side by side.
real_world_anchor: Ruggles & Brodie (1947), 'An Empirical Approach to Economic Intelligence in World War II', Journal of the American Statistical Association: for mid-1940 to 1942, the statistical estimate was about 246 tanks per month versus intelligence estimates around 1,400; German records later showed about 245.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The 246/1,400/245 figures summarize a specific period; month-by-month estimates were less exact. The analysis relied mainly on gearbox serial numbers (and other component markings), not a single tank serial sequence.

title: What '95% Confident' Actually Means
hook: Most researchers asked about a 95% confidence interval endorse at least one false interpretation, such as 'there is a 95% chance the true value lies in this interval'. The 95% belongs to the method, not to any single interval.
core_insight: A 95% confidence procedure captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples; any one computed interval either contains it or does not. The randomness lives in the interval, not in the parameter.
key_visual: A fixed vertical line marks the true mean. Intervals rain down one at a time as horizontal bars, each from a fresh sample: green if it crosses the line, red if it misses; a counter settles near 95% green. The camera then freezes on one green and one red bar that look identical from the inside: from your single interval, you cannot tell which kind you have.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: build mean plus/minus 2 SD, forgetting to divide by sqrt(n); coverage is about 100% and the intervals are uselessly wide. Second try: mean plus/minus 1.96 SD/sqrt(n) with n = 5; coverage drops to about 88% because the SD is itself noisy. Fix: t-intervals. Measure coverage by simulation at every step.
real_world_anchor: Hoekstra, Morey, Rouder & Wagenmakers (2014), 'Robust Misinterpretation of Confidence Intervals', Psychonomic Bulletin & Review: students and researchers alike endorsed false statements about a CI at similar rates; the concept was introduced by Jerzy Neyman (1937).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: A Bayesian credible interval does support the 'probability the parameter is inside' reading; mention it so the contrast is fair. Coverage guarantees hold for the procedure under its assumptions (correct model, random sampling).

title: p < 0.05 Doesn't Mean You're 95% Sure
hook: If a field mostly tests long-shot ideas, a large share of its 'significant' results can be false even when everyone uses p < 0.05 honestly. With 1 in 10 tested hypotheses true and 80% power, over a third of discoveries are wrong.
core_insight: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true, not the probability that the null is true. How often a significant result is real depends on prior plausibility and power, exactly like a medical test's base rate.
key_visual: 1,000 hypothesis cards in a grid: 100 glow (true effects), 900 are dim. A testing sweep flips 80 of the true ones to 'significant' (power 0.8) and 45 of the nulls too (alpha 0.05). The non-significant cards fade, leaving 125 significant cards of which 45 are false, 36%. A final histogram shows p-values under the null are flat (uniform) while those from true effects pile up near zero.
build_fail_iterate: Naive reading: 'p = 0.03, so there is a 97% chance the effect is real.' Simulate a research field with a 10% prior and check the claim; it badly overstates. Then turn the prior and power knobs to show when significance is trustworthy, tying back to the base-rate grid of episode 2.
real_world_anchor: John Ioannidis (2005), 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False', PLoS Medicine; Open Science Collaboration (2015), 'Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science', Science: 97% of 100 original studies were significant but only 36% of the replications were.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The 36% false-discovery figure depends entirely on the assumed prior (10%) and power (80%); present it as an illustration, not a measured fact about any field. A failed replication does not prove the original was false, because replications have limited power too.

title: Why Small Studies Find Huge Effects
hook: When an underpowered study finds a statistically significant effect, the reported effect is almost guaranteed to be exaggerated, often several-fold. Passing the significance filter is what inflates it.
core_insight: Low power does not just cause missed effects: conditioning on significance selects the luckiest overestimates (Type M, magnitude, errors) and sometimes even the wrong sign (Type S errors).
key_visual: A bell-shaped sampling distribution centered on a small true effect, with significance thresholds as two walls at plus/minus 1.96 standard errors. Only the slivers beyond the walls survive; they lift out and their average is marked, far from the truth. As sample size grows, the bell narrows, more of it clears the walls, and a live 'exaggeration ratio' readout falls toward 1.
build_fail_iterate: Run 1,000 simulated small studies of a real but small effect (say d = 0.2 with 20 per group) and 'publish' only the significant ones. A meta-analysis of the published set reports an effect several times too large. Fix: adequately powered, pre-registered designs and publishing null results; rerun and watch the bias vanish.
real_world_anchor: Button et al. (2013), 'Power Failure: Why Small Sample Size Undermines the Reliability of Neuroscience', Nature Reviews Neuroscience, estimated median statistical power in the neuroscience studies they examined at about 21%; Gelman & Carlin (2014), Perspectives on Psychological Science, defined Type S and Type M errors.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The exaggeration ratio depends on the true effect and the standard error; quote a ratio only alongside its simulation setup. Power is a property of a design for a hypothesized effect size, not of an observed result; avoid 'post-hoc power'.

title: The Dead Fish That Lit Up an fMRI Scanner
hook: Researchers put a dead Atlantic salmon in an fMRI scanner, showed it photos of people in social situations, and found 'significant' brain activity. The fish was not thinking; the statistics were.
core_insight: Run enough tests and some will come up significant by chance; with tens of thousands of voxels tested at once, false positives are guaranteed unless you correct for multiple comparisons (family-wise error or false discovery rate).
key_visual: A 3-D grid of voxels shaped like a fish. Every voxel independently rolls a weighted die; a handful glow red at the uncorrected threshold and happen to form plausible-looking blobs. A slider applies Bonferroni and then Benjamini-Hochberg corrections and the red voxels wink out. A side panel plots P(at least one false positive) = 1 - (1 - alpha)^m racing toward 1 as m grows.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: test every voxel at p < 0.05; hundreds light up. Tighten to p < 0.001 with a small cluster-size rule; a few blobs survive in the dead fish. Fix: proper family-wise or FDR correction, then show the trade-off with power on a simulated real signal.
real_world_anchor: Bennett, Baird, Miller & Wolford (poster 2009; Journal of Serendipitous and Unexpected Results, 2010), 'Neural Correlates of Interspecies Perspective Taking in the Post-Mortem Atlantic Salmon'; awarded the 2012 Ig Nobel Prize in Neuroscience. The apparent activity disappeared after multiple-comparisons correction.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The study was a deliberate demonstration of a statistical problem, not a debunking of fMRI; properly corrected analyses remain valid. The uncorrected analysis used p < 0.001 with a minimum cluster of 3 voxels; describe it accurately.

title: The Lady Who Could Taste Milk-First Tea
hook: One of statistics' most famous experiments began with a scientist who claimed she could taste whether milk or tea had been poured first. The test Fisher designed for her needs no formulas at all, just counting arrangements.
core_insight: If the null hypothesis says the labels do not matter, then shuffling the labels generates the exact distribution of your statistic under the null; the p-value is where your real result falls in that shuffled distribution.
key_visual: Eight teacups in a row, four secretly milk-first. All 70 ways to pick four cups fan out as mini-rows sorted by how many milk-first cups they catch, stacking into the counts 1, 16, 36, 16, 1. Then a larger dataset: two groups of dots whose color labels are shuffled again and again, each shuffle dropping a difference in means onto a growing histogram, with the real difference marked as a spike far in the tail.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: run a t-test on eight binary judgments; its assumptions are clearly broken. Fix: enumerate all 70 arrangements for an exact p-value (1/70, about 0.014, for a perfect score). Scale up: when enumeration is impossible, shuffle 10,000 times at random, and check that the Monte Carlo p-value matches the exact one on the small case.
real_world_anchor: R. A. Fisher, The Design of Experiments (1935), Chapter 2, inspired by Dr. Muriel Bristol at Rothamsted Experimental Station.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Whether Bristol actually identified all eight cups is anecdotal (reported later, e.g. in Salsburg's The Lady Tasting Tea, 2001); say 'reportedly'. Permutation tests assume exchangeability under the null; they do not fix confounding or non-random assignment.

title: The Bootstrap: Error Bars From Your Own Data
hook: You have one sample and no formula for the uncertainty of your statistic, say a median or a correlation. Resampling your own data with replacement, thousands of times, gives a remarkably good answer.
core_insight: Treat the sample as a stand-in for the population: resampling it mimics drawing fresh samples, so the spread of the recomputed statistic approximates its sampling distribution.
key_visual: Fifteen data points as marbles in a bag. A mechanical arm draws 15 times with replacement, duplicates glowing; the statistic is computed and dropped as a block onto a histogram. Thousands of draws fast-forward into a smooth bootstrap distribution, overlaid on the true sampling distribution computed from the known simulated population.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: resample without replacement; every resample is identical and the spread is zero. Fix: sample with replacement. Then break it on purpose: bootstrap the sample maximum. About 63% of resamples contain the observed maximum, producing a spike that badly misrepresents the truth. Lesson: the bootstrap works for smooth statistics, not for extremes.
real_world_anchor: Bradley Efron (1979), 'Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife', Annals of Statistics; the classic teaching example bootstraps the LSAT-GPA correlation across 15 American law schools (Efron & Tibshirani, An Introduction to the Bootstrap, 1993).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The bootstrap needs a reasonably representative sample of independent observations; time series and clustered data need block or cluster bootstraps. It does not create information, and with n = 15 its intervals are only approximate.

title: How Bayes Found a Plane at the Bottom of the Ocean
hook: Air France 447 vanished into the Atlantic in 2009, and two years of searching found nothing. A Bayesian reanalysis that treated every failed search as evidence pointed to where the wreck was found about a week after the search resumed.
core_insight: Bayesian updating combines prior beliefs with evidence, including negative evidence: not finding something lowers, but does not zero, the probability where you looked, in proportion to how likely you were to find it there.
key_visual: An ocean grid rendered as a glowing heat map: the prior built from the last known position and drift models. Search swaths sweep across in phases; each swept cell dims by its miss probability while unsearched cells brighten as probability renormalizes. Then one assumption flips, 'the underwater beacons may have failed', and cells near the last known position, previously searched only acoustically, brighten again.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: mark searched cells as 'cleared' (probability zero) and move on; the search drifts ever farther away. Fix 1: multiply by the probability of missing rather than zeroing. Fix 2: put uncertainty on the detection model itself (beacon failure), which revives the high-prior region near the last known position.
real_world_anchor: Stone, Keller, Kratzke & Strumpfer (2014), 'Search for the Wreckage of Air France Flight AF 447', Statistical Science: Metron's 2011 Bayesian posterior map; the wreckage was located in April 2011 close to the last known position, in a high-probability area.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Do not claim Bayes alone found the plane; sonar vehicles, search crews and earlier work mattered. The key modeling insight was allowing for beacon failure, which explained why earlier acoustic searches near the last known position had heard nothing.

title: How to Sample From a Shape You Can't Normalize
hook: Bayesian posteriors usually contain an integral nobody can compute. In 1953, scientists at Los Alamos found a way around it: a random walker that only ever compares heights and never needs the total.
core_insight: A Markov chain designed so its long-run distribution equals the target (always accept uphill moves, accept downhill moves with probability equal to the height ratio) samples a distribution known only up to a constant.
key_visual: A 2-D density rendered as glowing contour terrain, a banana-shaped posterior. A walker proposes jumps as ghost arrows: uphill always accepted, downhill accepted by a visible dice roll. Its footprints accumulate into a point cloud whose histogram converges to the terrain. Side by side: three walkers with too-small, too-large and well-tuned step sizes.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: evaluate the posterior on a grid and normalize; fine in 2-D, impossible in 50-D. Next: rejection sampling, whose acceptance rate collapses in high dimension. Then Metropolis: it works, but tiny steps wander slowly and huge steps are mostly rejected. Tune the step size by acceptance rate and check convergence with multiple chains (R-hat).
real_world_anchor: Metropolis, Rosenbluth, Rosenbluth, Teller & Teller (1953), 'Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines', Journal of Chemical Physics, run on Los Alamos's MANIAC computer; generalized by W. K. Hastings (1970), Biometrika.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: MCMC draws are autocorrelated and early draws reflect the starting point, so the effective sample size is smaller than the number of draws. Credit is shared: Arianna and Marshall Rosenbluth did much of the algorithmic and coding work; avoid crediting Metropolis alone.

title: A Dinosaur Hiding in Your Summary Statistics
hook: A cloud of points shaped like a dinosaur and a cloud shaped like a star can share the same means, standard deviations and correlation to two decimal places. Summary statistics can hide everything that matters.
core_insight: Very different datasets can share identical summary statistics; always plot the data, because means, variances and correlations compress away structure.
key_visual: About 140 points arranged as a T. rex slide smoothly into a star, then a circle, then parallel lines, while a live readout of mean x, mean y, SD x, SD y and correlation stays frozen to two decimals. Then Anscombe's four panels appear with their identical fitted regression lines.
build_fail_iterate: Build the morph yourself: nudge points randomly toward a target shape and keep only nudges that leave the statistics within tolerance. Version 1 lets the statistics drift; version 2 rejects every statistic-changing move and gets stuck; version 3 adds simulated annealing to escape. Measure how close each version gets to the target shape.
real_world_anchor: Matejka & Fitzmaurice (2017), 'Same Stats, Different Graphs: Generating Datasets with Varied Appearance and Identical Statistics through Simulated Annealing', CHI 2017 (original Datasaurus drawn by Alberto Cairo, 2016); F. J. Anscombe (1973), 'Graphs in Statistical Analysis', The American Statistician.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The statistics match to two decimal places, not exactly. Anscombe's quartet is four datasets of 11 points each; the Datasaurus Dozen is 13 datasets; do not mix them up.

title: When Every Part Says Yes but the Whole Says No
hook: In 1973, UC Berkeley's graduate admissions looked biased against women: about 44% of men were admitted versus 35% of women. Yet department by department, women were admitted at similar or higher rates.
core_insight: Aggregated rates can reverse the direction of subgroup rates when group sizes differ across a lurking variable (here, which departments people applied to); whether to aggregate depends on the causal story.
key_visual: Simpson's paradox as vector addition: each department is an arrow (x = applicants, y = admits) whose slope is its admission rate. In each department the women's arrow is at least as steep as the men's, but the women's longest arrows point into low-slope, competitive departments, so the summed women's vector ends up shallower than the summed men's vector.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: compare overall admission rates and declare bias. Iterate: split by department and watch the reversal. Then show 'always disaggregate' is not a rule either: build a second example where the third variable is a consequence of the treatment (a mediator), in which the aggregate is the right comparison. The causal graph decides.
real_world_anchor: Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell (1975), 'Sex Bias in Graduate Admissions: Data from Berkeley', Science: fall 1973 applications from about 8,400 men and 4,300 women; women disproportionately applied to departments with low admission rates.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Bickel et al. found a small department-level bias in favor of women, not proof that no discrimination existed anywhere (for example, why some fields were more competitive). The famous six-department table is a subset of the roughly 85 departments analysed.

title: How Selection Creates Correlations Out of Nothing
hook: Among hospital patients, two completely unrelated diseases can look negatively correlated, as if having one protects you from the other. Nothing about the biology changed; the hospital's front door did it.
core_insight: Selecting a sample on a combination of two variables (admitted if A or B is severe enough) induces a spurious association between them. This is Berkson's paradox, a special case of collider bias.
key_visual: A square of uniformly scattered points: two independent traits with zero correlation. A diagonal 'admission line' slides in and only points above it (A + B high enough) stay lit. The lit triangle has an obvious negative slope and a regression line snaps onto it. Moving the threshold strengthens and weakens the fake correlation.
build_fail_iterate: Naive analysis of hospital records finds that disease A 'protects' against disease B. Simulate a population where A and B are independent, apply the admission rule, and reproduce the fake effect. Fix: sample from the general population or model the selection mechanism explicitly, and watch the correlation vanish.
real_world_anchor: Joseph Berkson (1946), 'Limitations of the Application of Fourfold Table Analysis to Hospital Data', Biometrics Bulletin; modern example: Griffith et al. (2020), 'Collider Bias Undermines Our Understanding of COVID-19 Disease Risk and Severity', Nature Communications, on tested or hospitalized samples suggesting smoking was protective.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Berkson's paradox requires selection that depends on both variables; filtering on one variable alone does not create it. Do not claim the smoking-COVID association was entirely collider bias; Griffith et al. present it as a plausible explanation that must be ruled out.

title: Armor Where the Bullet Holes Aren't
hook: Returning WWII bombers had bullet holes clustered on the wings and fuselage, so the obvious move was to armor those spots. The statistical insight: planes hit elsewhere, such as the engines, mostly did not come back to be counted.
core_insight: If your data contain only survivors, the absence of a pattern can be the strongest evidence; you have to model what happened to the units that never reached your dataset.
key_visual: A stylized, procedurally drawn aircraft silhouette. A thousand sorties spray uniformly random hit points onto planes; planes with engine hits fall off-screen. The survivors' hits stack onto one composite outline: dense on the wings, eerily empty on the engines. Then the lost planes fade back in and fill exactly those gaps.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: armor the most-hit regions and simulate the next campaign; losses barely change. Fix: estimate each region's lethality by comparing survivors' hit rates with the rates expected if hits were uniform; armor the under-hit regions, rerun, and watch losses drop.
real_world_anchor: Abraham Wald's 1943 memoranda for the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, analysed in Mangel & Samaniego (1984), 'Abraham Wald's Work on Aircraft Survivability', Journal of the American Statistical Association.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The famous red-dotted plane image is a modern illustration, not Wald's data, and the 'armor the engines' story is a simplification; Wald's work was a mathematical method for estimating vulnerability from damage on returning aircraft. Do not imply he single-handedly redesigned planes.

title: Why Praise Seems to Fail and Punishment Seems to Work
hook: Israeli flight instructors told Daniel Kahneman that praising a great landing made the next one worse, while shouting after a bad one made the next one better. They were seeing pure statistics.
core_insight: When an outcome mixes stable skill with luck, extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones, so any intervention applied right after extremes will look effective or harmful even if it does nothing.
key_visual: Galton's ellipse: a tilted cloud of parent and child heights. The SD line along the ellipse's long axis is drawn, then the regression line, visibly flatter. Vertical slices light up one by one and each slice's mean is marked; the means trace the regression line, always pulled toward the center. Then the axes are relabeled 'landing 1' and 'landing 2' and the same picture explains the instructors.
build_fail_iterate: Simulate pilots with fixed skill plus random luck. 'Praise' the top landings and 'criticize' the bottom ones, with both doing nothing at all. The before/after comparison 'proves' criticism works. Fix: a randomized control group of extreme performers who receive no feedback; they 'improve' and 'decline' by just as much.
real_world_anchor: Francis Galton (1886), 'Regression Towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature', Journal of the Anthropological Institute (928 adult children of 205 parent pairs); the flight-instructor story is in Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Regression to the mean does not shrink the population's spread over generations; it runs in both directions (tall children tend to have less tall parents too). It arises whenever the correlation is imperfect, from luck or from measurement error.

title: The Correlation That Flips When You Zoom In
hook: In 1930 U.S. census data, states with more immigrants had higher literacy rates. Yet individually, immigrants were slightly less likely to be literate than native-born Americans.
core_insight: Correlations between group averages (ecological correlations) can differ in size and even in sign from correlations among individuals; inferring individual behavior from aggregate data is the ecological fallacy.
key_visual: 48 translucent state bubbles on a plane (x = % foreign-born, y = % literate) forming an upward trend. The camera zooms into one bubble, which opens into individual dots in two colors; in every bubble the immigrant dots sit slightly lower. Zoom back out and the upward trend between bubbles reappears, explained by immigrants having settled in states where native-born literacy was high.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: regress state literacy on % foreign-born and conclude immigrants were more literate. Build a synthetic population that reproduces the state-level pattern while individuals show the opposite, and show the aggregate data alone cannot distinguish the two worlds. Fix: individual-level data, or ecological-inference methods with explicit, strong assumptions.
real_world_anchor: W. S. Robinson (1950), 'Ecological Correlations and the Behavior of Individuals', American Sociological Review: across the 48 states, % foreign-born and % illiterate correlated at about -0.53, while for individuals being foreign-born and being illiterate correlated at about +0.12.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Robinson reported correlations with illiteracy; keep the signs straight when re-expressing them as literacy. Aggregate data are not useless; the fallacy is the unwarranted jump from groups to individuals.

title: Redraw the Lines, Reverse the Result
hook: Take the same 99 Iowa counties and group them into six regions. Depending on where the borders go, the correlation between the elderly share of the population and the Republican vote can be pushed from about -0.99 to +0.99.
core_insight: Statistics computed on spatial aggregates depend on the size and shape of the units (the modifiable areal unit problem); the same individual data can support opposite conclusions after aggregation, the same engine that drives gerrymandering.
key_visual: A grid of 100 voter squares, 60 blue and 40 red. District boundaries morph like living cells: one map yields 3-2 blue, another 5-0 blue, another 3-2 red; same voters, three outcomes, with a seat counter ticking. Then a county map whose region borders reshuffle while a correlation dial swings between its extremes.
build_fail_iterate: Naive 'fair' districting: straight vertical strips; on clustered voters it still produces lopsided results. Optimize for compactness; still sensitive. Iterate to the modern approach: generate thousands of random valid districtings (ensemble or MCMC redistricting) and judge a proposed map against that distribution.
real_world_anchor: Openshaw & Taylor (1979), 'A Million or So Correlation Coefficients: Three Experiments on the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem', and Openshaw (1983), The Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (CATMOG 38): Iowa's 99 counties, % Republican vote versus % aged 60+ (r of about 0.34 at county level); six-zone aggregations could yield correlations from about -0.99 to +0.99.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The plus/minus 0.99 extremes come from deliberately optimized zonings; typical random zonings give a much narrower spread. The MAUP has two parts, scale (unit size) and zoning (unit shape and placement); name both.

title: When Missing Data Isn't Missing at Random
hook: Deleting rows with missing values feels like the cautious choice. But if high earners are the ones who skip the income question, every remaining average is biased, and filling the blanks with the mean makes your uncertainty look smaller than it is.
core_insight: What matters is why data are missing: completely at random (MCAR), at random given observed variables (MAR), or depending on the missing value itself (MNAR). The mechanism decides which fixes work.
key_visual: A complete scatter of age versus income. Three erasers sweep across it: MCAR removes random points and the fitted line does not move; MAR removes more young people's points, which conditioning on age can repair; MNAR removes the highest incomes and the line sinks. Then mean-imputed points snap onto a horizontal line, visibly flattening the cloud and shrinking its spread.
build_fail_iterate: Naive 1: listwise deletion gives biased means under MAR and MNAR. Naive 2: mean imputation preserves the mean under MCAR but shrinks variances and correlations. Better: multiple imputation from observed covariates, shown as ghost points jittering across imputations, which handles MAR. For MNAR there is no automatic fix; show a sensitivity-analysis band instead.
real_world_anchor: Donald B. Rubin (1976), 'Inference and Missing Data', Biometrika, which defined the MCAR/MAR/MNAR framework; multiple imputation in Rubin (1987), Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: MAR versus MNAR cannot be determined from the observed data alone; it is an assumption. MCAR is a strong condition that social data rarely satisfy.

title: Noisy Data Makes Real Effects Look Smaller
hook: Measure someone's blood pressure once and its link to stroke looks weaker than it really is. Random measurement error does not just add noise; it systematically flattens relationships.
core_insight: Random error in a predictor biases its estimated slope toward zero by the reliability ratio var(true)/var(observed), known as attenuation or regression dilution; error in the outcome only adds noise.
key_visual: A tight cloud around a steep line. Horizontal jitter is dialed up: points smear sideways and the fitted line visibly rotates flatter while the slope readout falls. Then vertical jitter instead: the cloud thickens but the line stays put. Finally a correction slider divides by the reliability and the line swings back.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: regress the outcome on one noisy measurement and report the slope. Iterate: measure twice, use the correlation between repeats to estimate reliability, apply Spearman's correction, and compare with the slope computed from the true values in the simulation.
real_world_anchor: Charles Spearman (1904), 'The Proof and Measurement of Association between Two Things', American Journal of Psychology; MacMahon et al. (1990), The Lancet, showed that correcting for regression dilution substantially strengthened the estimated associations of blood pressure with stroke and coronary heart disease.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Clean attenuation holds for classical random error in a single predictor; with several predictors, error in one can bias the others in either direction. Systematic (non-random) error can bias estimates away from zero.

title: When a Measure Becomes a Target
hook: In 1902, colonial Hanoi paid a bounty for every rat tail handed in. Officials soon noticed tailless rats in the streets: people were cutting off tails and letting the rats go on breeding.
core_insight: Optimizing a proxy pulls it away from the goal it was meant to track: under pressure, the cheapest way to move the number diverges from the thing you actually care about (Goodhart's and Campbell's laws).
key_visual: Two overlapping landscapes, a 'true goal' surface and a 'proxy' surface that agree near the starting point. A ball climbs the proxy by gradient ascent; at first both scores rise together on a live plot, then the paths separate and the true score falls while the proxy keeps climbing.
build_fail_iterate: Build an optimizer rewarded for a metric (rat tails delivered, or a model scored on a proxy) and watch it find loopholes. Patch it: multiple metrics, caps, audits. Each patch closes one exploit and the agent finds the next, showing why metrics need ongoing judgment rather than a single clever fix.
real_world_anchor: Michael G. Vann (2003), 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race: The Great Hanoi Rat Massacre, an Episode in French Colonial History', French Colonial History; Charles Goodhart (1975) on monetary targets; the popular wording 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' is Marilyn Strathern's (1997) paraphrase.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Attribute the quoted wording to Strathern, not to Goodhart. Use the documented Hanoi rat bounty rather than the 'cobra effect' story from British India, which is poorly sourced.

title: Linear Regression Is Just a Shadow
hook: Fitting a line through 1,000 points looks like a messy optimization. Geometrically it is a single right angle: the fitted values are the shadow of your data vector on a flat plane in 1,000-dimensional space.
core_insight: Least squares finds the point in the space spanned by the predictors that is closest to the outcome vector; the residual is perpendicular to every predictor, which is why residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with each predictor.
key_visual: Start with just 3 data points so the outcome vector y lives in 3-D. The intercept column and the x column span a plane; y floats above it. A light shines straight down and y's shadow on the plane is y-hat, with the dashed residual dropping at a right angle. Cut to the familiar 2-D scatter where the same fit appears as a line, linked by color.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: fit by eye, or minimize absolute vertical errors by trial and error; unstable. Try minimizing perpendicular distances instead; a different line appears (total least squares), so 'best fit' needs a definition. Settle on squared vertical errors and derive the normal equations from 'residual perpendicular to the plane'. Fail: add a duplicate predictor and the plane degenerates (collinearity).
real_world_anchor: Carl Friedrich Gauss used least squares to predict where the newly discovered and then lost dwarf planet Ceres would reappear; it was recovered on 31 December 1801 close to his prediction. Legendre published the method first (1805); Gauss published in 1809.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Regressing y on x and x on y give different lines, because least squares minimizes vertical distances only. There is a priority dispute: Legendre published first, while Gauss claimed earlier use.

title: Why a Perfect Fit Is a Warning Sign
hook: John von Neumann reportedly quipped that with four parameters he could fit an elephant, and with five make it wiggle its trunk. In 2010, physicists actually did it, a reminder that fitting your data perfectly says nothing about predicting new data.
core_insight: Expected prediction error = bias squared + variance + irreducible noise. Flexible models cut bias but raise variance, so training error keeps falling while error on new data eventually rises.
key_visual: Ten noisy points from a smooth curve; polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 9 are fitted and the degree-9 curve snakes through every point. Then 50 fresh datasets are drawn and all 50 fits overlaid for each degree: degree 1 is a tight bundle of wrong lines (bias), degree 9 is wild spaghetti (variance). A U-shaped test-error curve draws itself underneath while training error slides to zero.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: choose complexity by training error; it always picks the most complex model, which then fails on held-out data. Fix: a held-out set reveals the U-curve. Compute bias squared and variance explicitly from the 50 resamples and show that they (plus the noise) add up to the test error.
real_world_anchor: Freeman Dyson (2004), 'A Meeting with Enrico Fermi', Nature, recounting Fermi quoting von Neumann; Mayer, Khairy & Howard (2010), 'Drawing an Elephant with Four Complex Parameters', American Journal of Physics.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Mayer et al. used four complex parameters (eight real numbers) plus a fifth for the trunk wiggle; say so. Heavily over-parameterized models can show 'double descent', with test error falling again past the interpolation point, so the U-curve is not universal; mention it as a teaser.

title: Why the Lasso Has Sharp Corners
hook: Add a penalty and your model fits its training data worse, on purpose, yet predicts new data better. One kind of penalty also sets many coefficients exactly to zero, for a purely geometric reason: diamonds have corners.
core_insight: Regularization trades a little bias for less variance. The L1 (lasso) constraint region is a diamond whose corners sit on the axes, so the optimum often lands where some coefficients are exactly zero; the L2 (ridge) region is round, so it shrinks coefficients but rarely zeros them.
key_visual: In coefficient space (beta1, beta2), elliptical contours of the squared-error loss grow outward from the least-squares point until they first touch a constraint region: a circle (ridge), touched on a smooth edge, and a diamond (lasso), touched at a corner on an axis. As the constraint shrinks, the lasso path snaps coefficients to zero one at a time, shown as a coefficient-path plot.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: ordinary least squares with 50 predictors and 60 observations; huge, unstable coefficients and poor test error. Add ridge: stable, but all 50 predictors kept. Add lasso: a sparse model with better test error. Tune the penalty by cross-validation and plot test error against penalty strength.
real_world_anchor: Robert Tibshirani (1996), 'Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the Lasso', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B; Hoerl & Kennard (1970) introduced ridge regression; Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, illustrate the lasso on the Stamey et al. prostate cancer data.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Variables the lasso selects are not necessarily the true causes; with correlated predictors its choice among them is somewhat arbitrary. Standardize predictors before penalizing, or the penalty depends on measurement units.

title: The Cross-Validation Mistake That Fooled Biologists
hook: With 50 samples and 5,000 pure-noise features, you can build a classifier whose cross-validated error looks close to zero while its true error is 50%. All it takes is choosing the features before you cross-validate.
core_insight: Every step that learns from data, including feature selection, tuning and preprocessing, must happen inside each cross-validation fold; otherwise the held-out data have already leaked into the model.
key_visual: The dataset as a tall stack of rows split into five fold-bands. Wrong way: a 'feature selector' beam scans the entire stack, test folds included, then cross-validation runs and a scoreboard shows about 3% error. Right way: the beam is confined to the training folds and reruns for each fold; the scoreboard jumps to about 50%. A ghost overlay shows exactly what information crossed the wall.
build_fail_iterate: Build the pipeline naively on random labels and 'discover' a near-perfect gene signature. Suspect it: rerun with labels shuffled; still near-perfect, a red flag. Fix: nest feature selection inside each fold (and use nested CV for hyperparameters); the error returns to chance.
real_world_anchor: Ambroise & McLachlan (2002), 'Selection Bias in Gene Extraction on the Basis of Microarray Gene-Expression Data', PNAS; the 50-sample, 5,000-feature demonstration is in Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 7.10.2.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: In the ESL example the wrong-way CV error was about 3% versus a true 50%; exact numbers vary by simulation, so label yours as a simulation. Unsupervised steps that never see labels (like scaling) leak much less, but in principle should also be fitted within folds.

title: Why Gradient Descent Zigzags
hook: Gradient descent always steps in the steepest downhill direction, and that is exactly why it can take thousands of steps to cross a narrow valley, bouncing from wall to wall instead of heading for the bottom.
core_insight: The gradient points steepest-downhill locally, not toward the minimum. On ill-conditioned surfaces (long, thin valleys) fixed-step descent zigzags and too large a step diverges; momentum, adaptive steps and rescaling features fix much of this.
key_visual: A glowing contour map of a long, curved valley (Rosenbrock's banana function). Balls roll by plain gradient descent: a tiny step creeps, a big step ricochets off-screen, a medium step zigzags. A momentum ball with a fading trail glides along the valley floor. A side plot shows loss versus iteration on a log scale for each.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: learning rate 1; the loss diverges to infinity. Shrink to 0.0001; it crawls. Tune it; it zigzags. Add momentum; much faster. Finally rescale the axes (standardize features) so the valley becomes round, and plain descent improves dramatically.
real_world_anchor: Augustin-Louis Cauchy proposed steepest descent in 1847; Howard Rosenbrock's 'banana' test function appeared in The Computer Journal (1960); Boris Polyak (1964) introduced the heavy-ball (momentum) method.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The zigzag is a property of fixed or poorly chosen step sizes on ill-conditioned problems; with exact line search successive steps are orthogonal. In deep learning, stochastic gradients add noise that is partly helpful; do not conflate that with full-batch behavior.

title: Why a Forest of Bad Trees Beats One Good Tree
hook: A single carefully grown decision tree memorizes noise. Grow hundreds of trees deliberately crippled by randomness, each seeing a random sample and random features, and their vote is far more accurate.
core_insight: Deep trees have low bias but high variance. Averaging many trees reduces variance, and forcing diversity (bootstrap samples plus random feature subsets at each split) decorrelates the trees so the averaging actually helps.
key_visual: Two-class data on a plane. One deep tree carves axis-aligned rectangles, including tiny boxes around individual noisy points. Then 200 trees' boundaries are overlaid, each at 0.5% opacity; the jagged boxes blur into a smooth, accurate boundary. A meter shows prediction variance falling as trees are added and leveling off at a floor set by the correlation between trees.
build_fail_iterate: Grow one tree by information gain (the entropy of episode 7): 100% training accuracy, poor test accuracy. Prune it: better but rigid. Bag 100 trees on bootstrap samples: better, but they all split first on the same strong feature, so they stay correlated. Add random feature subsets at each split to get a random forest, and plot test error against the number of trees.
real_world_anchor: Leo Breiman (2001), 'Random Forests', Machine Learning, building on bagging (Breiman, 1996); Shotton et al. (2011), CVPR, used randomized decision forests for real-time body-part recognition in Microsoft's Kinect.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Averaging reduces variance, not bias; a forest cannot rescue a fundamentally uninformative feature set. The variance floor (rho times sigma squared) is why decorrelating the trees through feature subsampling matters.

title: Turning Barely-Better-Than-Chance Rules Into an Expert
hook: In the late 1980s, theorists asked whether a pile of rules of thumb, each only slightly better than guessing, could be combined into an arbitrarily accurate classifier. The answer was yes, and the idea later powered the first real-time face detectors.
core_insight: Boosting builds a model sequentially: each new weak learner concentrates on the examples the current ensemble gets wrong (by reweighting them or fitting the residuals), steadily driving down bias.
key_visual: Points on a plane; one 'decision stump' (a single straight cut) misclassifies many. Misclassified points swell in size as their weights grow. The next stump cuts to catch the big points; those it fixes shrink, others swell. After 50 rounds the weighted vote of stumps forms an intricate boundary. A side panel shows gradient boosting as successive fits to residuals stacking up into a curve.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: average many identical stumps; no improvement, because there is no diversity. Fix: reweight the mistakes (AdaBoost) and accuracy climbs. Fail: add label noise and boosting obsessively chases the mislabeled points and overfits. Fix: shrinkage (a small learning rate), early stopping and more robust loss functions.
real_world_anchor: Kearns & Valiant posed the weak-learnability question (1988-89); Robert Schapire (1990) proved boosting is possible; Freund & Schapire (1997) introduced AdaBoost; Viola & Jones (2001) used boosted simple image features for real-time face detection.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: 'Boosting reduces bias, forests reduce variance' is a useful contrast, not an absolute rule. AdaBoost is sensitive to label noise; modern gradient-boosting libraries add regularization to cope.

title: Separating the Inseparable by Adding a Dimension
hook: Some data cannot be split by any straight line, like a red cluster surrounded by a blue ring. Lift the points into a third dimension and a flat sheet separates them perfectly, and a kernel lets you do this without ever computing the new coordinates.
core_insight: Support vector machines find the boundary with the widest margin, which depends only on the closest points (support vectors) and only through dot products; replacing dot products with a kernel implicitly maps the data into a higher-dimensional space where a linear separator exists.
key_visual: A 2-D disk of red points inside a blue ring. The points lift onto the paraboloid z = x^2 + y^2: reds stay low, blues rise. A horizontal plane slides between them, and projecting it back down draws a perfect circle in the original view. Then the max-margin 'street' between the classes appears, with the points on its gutters (the support vectors) glowing.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: a perceptron in 2-D cycles forever on the ring data. Fix 1: hand-craft the x^2 + y^2 feature; it works but needs foresight. Fix 2: the kernel trick (an RBF kernel) does it automatically. Fail: an RBF kernel that is too narrow wraps little islands around every point and overfits; tune C and gamma by cross-validation.
real_world_anchor: Boser, Guyon & Vapnik (1992), COLT, introduced kernelized maximum-margin classifiers; Cortes & Vapnik (1995), 'Support-Vector Networks', Machine Learning, added soft margins and demonstrated the method on handwritten-digit recognition.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The kernel computes inner products in the feature space without constructing it; for the RBF kernel that space is infinite-dimensional. A maximum margin is a regularization principle, not a guarantee of the best accuracy.

title: k-means Will Find Clusters in Pure Noise
hook: Give k-means uniformly random points and ask for five clusters, and it will confidently return five tidy groups. Clustering algorithms always find clusters; whether they are real is a separate question.
core_insight: k-means alternates between assigning points to the nearest center and moving each center to the mean of its points, minimizing within-cluster variance. It assumes round, similar-sized clusters, depends on initialization, and partitions whatever it is given.
key_visual: Voronoi cells bloom around five centroid stars; points recolor to their cell; the stars glide to their cells' centers of mass; the cells re-tile; repeat until nothing moves. Run it on clear blobs (great), on two interlocking crescents (sliced wrongly) and on uniform noise (five confident slices). A gap-statistic meter compares each result with data that has no clusters.
build_fail_iterate: Naive random initialization drops two centers into one blob and none into another, stuck in a local optimum. Fix: k-means++ seeding and multiple restarts. Next failure: the crescents. Iterate to density-based or spectral clustering. Final check: compare cluster quality against reference data simulated with no clusters (the gap statistic).
real_world_anchor: Stuart Lloyd's algorithm (Bell Labs memo, 1957; published 1982 in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory) for quantizing signals; the name 'k-means' is from MacQueen (1967); Arthur & Vassilvitskii (2007) introduced k-means++; Tibshirani, Walther & Hastie (2001) proposed the gap statistic.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: k-means finds a local, not necessarily global, minimum (the global problem is NP-hard). Results depend on feature scaling: standardize, or the variable with the largest units dominates.

title: Genes That Draw a Map of Europe
hook: Take genetic data from people across Europe and apply a method that knows nothing about geography. The first two directions of variation, plotted against each other, look strikingly like a map of Europe.
core_insight: PCA rotates the data to find orthogonal directions of maximum variance (the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix); projecting onto the top few compresses high-dimensional data while keeping most of its spread.
key_visual: A 3-D cloud of points shaped like a rugby ball. The coordinate axes rotate until the first aligns with the longest stretch and the second with the next; the cloud flattens onto the PC1-PC2 plane while variance bars (a scree plot) rise beside each axis. Then thousands of points, each a simulated person colored by a schematic country, settle into the outline of Europe on the PC plane.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: pick two raw features to plot; little structure appears. Run PCA without centering or scaling; the first component just tracks the feature with the biggest units. Fix: center (and scale where appropriate). Fail: PCA on a smooth spatial gradient produces wave-like components that can be mistaken for migrations; interpret with care.
real_world_anchor: Novembre et al. (2008), 'Genes Mirror Geography within Europe', Nature; PCA dates to Karl Pearson (1901) and Harold Hotelling (1933). Novembre & Stephens (2008), Nature Genetics, warned that PCA patterns can arise from simple spatial structure.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The map emerged after restricting to individuals with grandparents from the same country, removing outliers, and rotating the PC axes; mention this processing. Principal components are directions of variance, not necessarily meaningful 'factors' or specific historical events.

title: What a t-SNE Plot Can't Tell You
hook: In a t-SNE or UMAP plot, the size of a cluster and the distance between clusters can be essentially meaningless, and with the wrong settings pure noise can come out looking like islands.
core_insight: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local neighborhoods, not global geometry; densities get equalized and gaps between clusters get distorted, so these maps are for spotting neighbors, not for measuring distances or sizes.
key_visual: Three Gaussian blobs in 50 dimensions: one tight, one ten times wider, and a third much farther away. The t-SNE embedding animates iteration by iteration and ends with all three the same size and roughly evenly spaced. A perplexity slider morphs the output: low values shatter uniform noise into fake clumps, high values merge real clusters.
build_fail_iterate: Run t-SNE once with defaults and 'interpret' cluster sizes and gaps as biological or social facts. Rerun with different seeds and perplexities and the picture shifts. Fix: test on synthetic data with known structure, compare several perplexities, and measure distances in the original space or with PCA.
real_world_anchor: van der Maaten & Hinton (2008), 'Visualizing Data using t-SNE', Journal of Machine Learning Research; Wattenberg, Viegas & Johnson (2016), 'How to Use t-SNE Effectively', Distill; Chari & Pachter (2023), 'The Specious Art of Single-Cell Genomics', PLoS Computational Biology.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Do not claim t-SNE is useless; local neighborhoods are often meaningful. UMAP can preserve somewhat more global structure than t-SNE in some settings, but it still does not preserve distances.

title: A Neural Network Is Just a Pile of Bent Lines
hook: A famous 1969 book showed that a single-layer perceptron cannot even compute XOR. Add one hidden layer of simple 'bent lines' and a network can approximate essentially any continuous function.
core_insight: Each ReLU neuron is a line with a kink; a weighted sum of enough kinks can approximate any continuous curve (universal approximation). Hidden layers bend space so that tangled classes become separable by a straight line.
key_visual: The four XOR points on a plane; lines try every angle and fail to split them. A hidden layer warps the plane like a folded sheet until one line separates the classes. Then in 1-D: a target sine curve, with ReLU hinges added one by one, each bending a polyline closer until it traces the sine.
build_fail_iterate: Train a single perceptron on XOR; its weights oscillate forever. Add a hidden layer with linear activations; it still fails, because stacked linear maps are linear. Add a nonlinearity (ReLU); success. Then fit a sine with 2, 5 and 50 hidden units and watch the approximation improve.
real_world_anchor: Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958, Psychological Review); Marvin Minsky & Seymour Papert, Perceptrons (1969); universal approximation theorems by George Cybenko (1989) and Kurt Hornik (1991).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Minsky and Papert knew multilayer networks could represent XOR; their critique concerned single-layer perceptrons and the lack of a training method for deeper ones. Universal approximation guarantees existence, not that training will find the weights or that the network will be small.

title: How a Network Learns: Passing the Blame Backward
hook: A network with a million weights needs a million partial derivatives at every training step. Backpropagation gets all of them for roughly the cost of a couple of extra forward passes, not a million.
core_insight: Backprop is the chain rule applied in reverse order through a computational graph: each node receives the gradient of the loss with respect to its output and passes it back, scaled by its local derivative, reusing shared work.
key_visual: A small computational graph (inputs, multiply, add, ReLU, loss) drawn as glowing nodes. Forward pass: numbers flow left to right. Backward pass: a red 'blame' signal flows right to left, splitting at branches and multiplying by each local slope, and every weight lights up with its gradient. The camera pulls back to a multi-layer network as the red wave sweeps backward through the layers.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: estimate each gradient by nudging each weight and rerunning the network (finite differences); a cost counter explodes as weights are added, with numerical error to boot. Fix: reverse-mode chain rule. Fail: deep sigmoid networks, where the backward signal shrinks layer by layer (vanishing gradients). Fix: ReLU activations and careful initialization.
real_world_anchor: Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986), 'Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors', Nature, popularized backpropagation; reverse-mode automatic differentiation was described by Seppo Linnainmaa (1970) and applied to neural networks by Paul Werbos (1974, 1982).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Do not credit the invention solely to the 1986 paper. The cost advantage holds for a scalar loss (reverse mode); the trade-off is memory, because forward activations must be stored.

title: Attention: Every Word Asks Every Other Word a Question
hook: Early neural translation systems squeezed a whole sentence into one fixed-size vector before translating, and quality dropped on long sentences. Attention let each word look up every other word directly, and it became the core of modern language models.
core_insight: Attention is a soft, differentiable dictionary lookup: each token emits a query, compares it with every token's key by dot product, and takes a softmax-weighted average of their values, so context can flow directly between any two positions.
key_visual: A sentence as a row of glowing token orbs: 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired'. From 'it' a query arrow emerges; every token holds up a key arrow; dot products set the brightness of connecting beams; the softmax turns beams into weights that pour colored 'value' liquid back into 'it', mostly from 'animal'. Then the full attention matrix assembles row by row as a heat map.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: encode the sentence into one vector with a recurrent network; on a toy copy task, quality degrades with length. Fix 1: attention over all encoder states (Bahdanau). Fix 2: drop recurrence entirely and use self-attention with positional encodings (the Transformer), which also processes all positions in parallel.
real_world_anchor: Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio (2014; ICLR 2015), 'Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate'; Vaswani et al. (2017), 'Attention Is All You Need', NeurIPS.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Attention weights are not reliable explanations of a model's decisions (Jain & Wallace, 2019). Without positional information, self-attention ignores word order, so order must be injected separately. The 'it' to 'animal' pattern is illustrative; real attention heads vary.

title: 99.8% Accurate and Completely Useless
hook: In a widely used credit-card dataset, only 0.17% of transactions are fraud. A model that flags nothing is 99.8% accurate, and a model with an impressive ROC curve can still bury investigators in false alarms.
core_insight: With rare positives, accuracy and even ROC-AUC can look excellent while precision is terrible; precision-recall curves and the real costs of each error type reveal what matters. Every threshold is a trade-off.
key_visual: Two overlapping score distributions, a small red hill (fraud) and a blue mountain (legitimate). A threshold line slides across; each position plots a point on the ROC curve, which hugs the top-left corner, and simultaneously on the precision-recall curve, which collapses. Then the blue mountain is redrawn at true scale, dwarfing the red hill, making it obvious why a tiny false-positive rate still means a flood of false alarms.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: optimize accuracy; the model predicts 'no fraud' for everything. Fix 1: class weights or resampling; it catches fraud but floods analysts with alerts. Fix 2: choose the threshold from the PR curve and a cost matrix (missed fraud versus analyst time). Note that resampling distorts predicted probabilities, which then need recalibration (next episode).
real_world_anchor: Dal Pozzolo et al. (2015), 'Calibrating Probability with Undersampling for Unbalanced Classification', IEEE SSCI, describing the ULB/Worldline credit-card dataset (284,807 transactions, 492 frauds); Saito & Rehmsmeier (2015), PLoS ONE, on why precision-recall plots are more informative than ROC for imbalanced data.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: ROC-AUC is insensitive to class balance, which is useful for ranking but hides precision problems; do not call ROC 'wrong'. The baseline precision for a PR curve is the positive rate (about 0.0017), not 0.5.

title: When 90% Confident Isn't 90% Right
hook: Modern deep neural networks are far more accurate than those of the 1990s, yet many are worse at knowing when they are wrong: when they say 90%, they can be right much less often.
core_insight: A calibrated model's stated probabilities match observed frequencies. Accuracy and calibration are different properties, and simple post-hoc fixes such as temperature scaling can restore calibration without changing which class is predicted.
key_visual: A reliability diagram: predictions sorted into confidence bins as stacked tiles, each column rising to the observed accuracy in that bin, with the perfect-calibration diagonal glowing. The overconfident network's columns sit below the diagonal. A 'temperature' knob turns, softmax outputs soften, and the columns slide up onto the diagonal while the accuracy counter stays fixed.
build_fail_iterate: Train a large network until its training loss is tiny; check accuracy (great) and calibration (poor). Naive fix: retrain a smaller model, which loses accuracy. Better: hold out data and fit a single temperature parameter (or isotonic regression), then measure expected calibration error before and after.
real_world_anchor: Guo, Pleiss, Sun & Weinberger (2017), 'On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks', ICML, e.g. a 110-layer ResNet was much more accurate but far less calibrated than a 1998 LeNet on CIFAR-100; Murphy & Winkler (1977), Applied Statistics, showed U.S. weather forecasters' precipitation probabilities were well calibrated.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Calibration must be measured on held-out data and can break under distribution shift. Guo et al. describe a trend in the architectures and training practices they studied; not every modern model is overconfident.

title: The Machine Learning Bug Hiding in Hundreds of Papers
hook: Several published papers claimed machine learning predicted civil wars far better than old-fashioned logistic regression. When researchers corrected data leakage and other errors, the advantage disappeared.
core_insight: Leakage happens when information that would not be available at prediction time (future data, duplicated records, or statistics computed on the test set) sneaks into training, producing spectacular but fake performance.
key_visual: Training and test sets as two rooms separated by a wall, with data rows as glowing packets. Three leaks animate as cracks: a feature recorded after the event travels backward along a timeline; duplicate rows appear in both rooms; preprocessing statistics are computed across the wall. An accuracy meter drops each time a crack is sealed.
build_fail_iterate: Build a model that predicts an event using a feature recorded after the event; performance is near-perfect. Audit: check feature timestamps, split by time and train on the past only; the edge vanishes. Install the fix: time-based splits, de-duplication, and a leakage checklist.
