real_world_anchor: Kapoor & Narayanan (2023), 'Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in Machine-Learning-Based Science', Patterns: found leakage affecting at least 294 papers across 17 fields, and in civil-war prediction showed complex models did not outperform logistic regression once errors were fixed; Kaufman et al. (2012), 'Leakage in Data Mining', ACM TKDD.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The 294 figure comes from Kapoor & Narayanan's survey of errors reported across fields; present it as 'at least'. Leakage is usually an honest pipeline mistake, not misconduct.

title: Your Image Classifier Might Be Reading the Copyright Notice
hook: A well-performing classifier recognized horses in photos, but an explanation method revealed it was largely keying on a small copyright tag that appeared on many of the horse pictures.
core_insight: High accuracy can rest on spurious shortcuts. Explanation tools (relevance heat maps, Shapley values) can expose what a model actually uses, but explanations are approximations that can mislead too.
key_visual: A procedurally drawn 'photo' (a geometric horse on a field) with a tiny text tag in one corner. A relevance heat map pours over it and almost all of it pools on the tag. Remove the tag and the prediction flips; paste the tag onto a car and the car becomes 'horse'. Then a Shapley-value bar chart assembles by averaging each feature's contribution over all coalitions of features.
build_fail_iterate: Train a toy classifier on synthetic images where one class always carries a corner watermark; test accuracy is about 100%. A saliency map lights up the watermark. Fix: remove or randomize the artifact, retrain, and test on data from a different source; report the honest, lower accuracy.
real_world_anchor: Lapuschkin et al. (2019), 'Unmasking Clever Hans Predictors and Assessing What Machines Really Learn', Nature Communications (horse class in PASCAL VOC relying on a source tag); Zech et al. (2018), PLoS Medicine, found pneumonia-detecting CNNs exploiting hospital-specific signals; the original Clever Hans, the 'counting' horse, was explained by Oskar Pfungst in 1907.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The popular 'husky versus wolf (snow)' example from Ribeiro et al. (2016, LIME) used a deliberately biased classifier built for a user study; do not present it as an accidental real-world failure. Saliency maps need sanity checks: some barely change when model weights are randomized (Adebayo et al., 2018).

title: Storks Deliver Babies (p = 0.008)
hook: Across 17 European countries, the number of breeding stork pairs is strongly correlated with the number of human births (r of about 0.62, p = 0.008). The correlation is real; the causation is not.
core_insight: A confounder causes both X and Y, creating correlation without causation. Causal diagrams (DAGs) make the assumptions explicit and tell you what to adjust for: block every back-door path.
key_visual: Countries as dots sized by land area, plotted storks versus births with a fitted line. A DAG assembles: a 'land area' node drops in with arrows to both 'storks' and 'births'. Conditioning on area slices the dots into area bands, and within each band the slope flattens. The back-door path lights up, then a gate closes on it.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: regress births on storks; significant. Add an irrelevant control; still significant. Draw the DAG, identify country size as the confounder, adjust, and the effect collapses. End with a warning that adjusting for everything is not safe either, a teaser for colliders in the next episode.
real_world_anchor: Robert Matthews (2000), 'Storks Deliver Babies (p = 0.008)', Teaching Statistics; the DAG framework is from Judea Pearl, Causality (2000; 2nd ed. 2009).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Matthews's dataset is a deliberate teaching example; the confounder he highlights is country size (land area). DAGs encode assumptions; they cannot discover causal structure from correlations alone.

title: When Controlling for a Variable Creates the Bias
hook: Among low-birth-weight babies, those born to mothers who smoked had lower infant mortality than those born to non-smokers. Smoking does not protect babies; conditioning on birth weight manufactured the paradox.
core_insight: Conditioning on a collider (a common effect of two causes) opens a spurious path between those causes, so 'controlling for more variables' can increase bias. Smoking and other, more dangerous causes both lead to low birth weight; among low-weight babies, smoking 'explains away' the more dangerous causes.
key_visual: A DAG: Smoking -> Low birth weight <- Birth defects (unmeasured), with Smoking and Defects both pointing to Mortality. A spotlight rings the 'low birth weight' node and a dashed red spurious link appears between Smoking and Defects. Then a population of baby icons sorted by cause: inside the low-weight box, smokers' babies are mostly 'smoking only' cases while non-smokers' babies are mostly higher-risk 'defect' cases.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: stratify by birth weight to 'isolate' smoking's effect and find a protective effect. Simulate a world where smoking is harmful and defects are worse, and reproduce the paradox exactly. Fix: do not condition on a variable that is a consequence of the exposure; estimate the total effect without adjusting for birth weight.
real_world_anchor: Hernandez-Diaz, Schisterman & Hernan (2006), 'The Birth Weight Paradox Uncovered?', American Journal of Epidemiology; the paradox was described earlier by Jacob Yerushalmy (1971).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Birth weight is both a mediator and a collider here; explain both roles. Hernandez-Diaz et al. show collider bias can explain the paradox under plausible assumptions; it is a model-based argument, not proof that nothing else matters.

title: When Observational Data Said the Opposite of the Trial
hook: Large observational studies suggested hormone therapy substantially cut heart-disease risk in postmenopausal women. When a big randomized trial tested estrogen plus progestin, it was stopped early, and the treated group had more coronary events, not fewer.
core_insight: Randomization balances all confounders, measured and unmeasured, on average, so differences between groups can be attributed to the treatment; observational comparisons can be distorted by who chooses treatment.
key_visual: A crowd of person icons, each with hidden 'health' and 'wealth' shading. In the observational world, a hand picks healthier-looking icons for treatment, and bar charts show the groups differ before treatment even starts. Then a coin flips over each icon and the groups' hidden-trait histograms match almost perfectly. The outcome bars flip direction between the two worlds.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: compare women who chose hormones with women who did not; protective effect. Adjust for measured confounders; still protective. Randomize; harm. Then reconcile: reanalyze the observational data as if emulating a trial (new users only, aligned start times) and the estimates move much closer to the trial's.
real_world_anchor: Writing Group for the Women's Health Initiative Investigators (Rossouw et al., 2002), JAMA: the estrogen-plus-progestin trial (16,608 women) was stopped early; observational benchmark: the Nurses' Health Study (e.g. Stampfer et al., 1991); reconciliation: Hernan et al. (2008), Epidemiology, target-trial emulation.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Later analyses suggest effects depend on age and time since menopause ('timing hypothesis'); do not say hormone therapy harms everyone. Hernan et al. found much of the discrepancy came from comparing long-term users and from timing, not only from 'healthy user' confounding.

title: Can Clever Statistics Replace a Randomized Experiment?
hook: In 1986, an economist took a job-training program whose effect was known from a randomized experiment and asked whether standard non-experimental methods could recover it. Most of them missed badly, some even getting the sign wrong.
core_insight: Matching and propensity-score methods compare treated units with similar untreated ones, but they can only balance observed covariates and need overlap; without the right covariates, sophisticated adjustment cannot recover an experimental benchmark.
key_visual: Treated units as orange dots and a huge cloud of untreated blue dots in a 2-D covariate space (age by prior earnings); most of the blue cloud sits far away. Lines snap from each orange dot to its nearest blue partner and unmatched blues fade. A balance plot shows covariate gaps shrinking. Then a propensity-score axis compresses many covariates into one, with the region of overlap highlighted.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: compare program participants with a general survey sample; the estimate is wildly negative. Add regression controls; still off. Propensity-score match on pre-program earnings; much closer to the experiment. Fail: change the sample or specification and the estimate swings. Lesson: check overlap and balance, and benchmark against experiments where possible.
real_world_anchor: Robert LaLonde (1986), 'Evaluating the Econometric Evaluations of Training Programs with Experimental Data', American Economic Review (National Supported Work Demonstration); Dehejia & Wahba (1999), JASA, came close with propensity scores; Smith & Todd (2005), Journal of Econometrics, showed that success was sensitive to sample choices.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Matching cannot fix unobserved confounding; Dehejia and Wahba's result depended on particular subsamples and on having two years of pre-program earnings. Present the debate rather than a verdict.

title: The Minimum Wage Study That Used New Jersey as a Lab
hook: Standard textbook models predicted that raising the minimum wage would cut fast-food jobs. When New Jersey raised its minimum wage in 1992, economists compared its restaurants with those across the border in Pennsylvania and found no drop in employment.
core_insight: Difference-in-differences compares the change over time in a treated group with the change in a control group; under 'parallel trends', the control group's change estimates what would have happened to the treated group.
key_visual: Two lines over time, New Jersey in orange and Pennsylvania in blue, crossing a vertical 'policy' line. A dashed ghost line extends New Jersey's path parallel to Pennsylvania's: the counterfactual. The gap between real and ghost New Jersey glows as the estimated effect. A second version with diverging pre-trends shows the ghost line clearly in the wrong place.
build_fail_iterate: Naive 1: New Jersey before versus after; confounded by anything else that changed over time. Naive 2: New Jersey versus Pennsylvania afterward; confounded by state differences. Fix: the difference of the differences. Stress test: plot several pre-policy periods (an event-study plot); if trends were not parallel before, the estimate is suspect.
real_world_anchor: Card & Krueger (1994), 'Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania', American Economic Review: New Jersey's minimum rose from $4.25 to $5.05 in April 1992; about 400 restaurants were surveyed. A precursor in spirit: John Snow's 1855 comparison of London water companies.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The finding was contested (Neumark & Wascher, 2000, using payroll records; Card & Krueger's 2000 reply); present it as a famous, debated case. Parallel trends after the policy is untestable; pre-trend checks are only suggestive. David Card shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Economics; Alan Krueger died in 2019.

title: What Happens the Night You Turn 21
hook: U.S. death rates jump by about 9% right after people turn 21, the legal drinking age. Because your exact birthday is unrelated to almost everything else about you, that jump is close to a natural experiment.
core_insight: When a treatment switches on at a threshold of some running variable, units just above and just below the threshold are comparable, so a jump in outcomes at the cutoff estimates the causal effect there.
key_visual: Mortality rates plotted by age in months from 19 to 23, with a vertical line at 21. Local linear fits approach the line from each side and leave a visible step. A bandwidth window narrows toward the cutoff and the step estimate stays stable. Then a high-order polynomial is fitted globally; it wiggles wildly near the edge and produces a fake jump, drawn in red.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: compare all 18-20-year-olds with all 21-24-year-olds; confounded by aging. Fix: local comparisons around 21. Fail: a global 6th-degree polynomial produces spurious jumps. Fix: local linear regression with a data-driven bandwidth, plus placebo cutoffs at 20 and 22 that should show no jump.
real_world_anchor: Carpenter & Dobkin (2009), 'The Effect of Alcohol Consumption on Mortality: Regression Discontinuity Evidence from the Minimum Drinking Age', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics: about a 9% increase in mortality at 21, driven mainly by motor-vehicle accidents, suicides and alcohol overdoses. Regression discontinuity was introduced by Thistlethwaite & Campbell (1960); polynomial cautions in Gelman & Imbens (2019).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: RDD estimates the effect at the cutoff (for people turning 21), not for all ages. The running variable must not be manipulable; birthdays are not, but test scores might be, so check for bunching at the cutoff (a density test).

title: A Lottery That Measured the Cost of War
hook: Did serving in Vietnam reduce men's later earnings? Comparing veterans with non-veterans is hopelessly confounded, but the draft lottery, which assigned risk of service by birthday, let an economist estimate it: about 15% lower earnings for white veterans in the early 1980s.
core_insight: An instrument shifts the treatment but affects the outcome only through the treatment; dividing its effect on the outcome by its effect on the treatment (the Wald ratio) estimates the causal effect for 'compliers', those whose treatment the instrument changed.
key_visual: A lottery drum spins and spits out birth dates; men split into 'low number' (likely drafted) and 'high number' groups. Two bars: veteran status jumps between the groups (arrow 1), earnings dip slightly (arrow 2). The IV estimate appears as the ratio of arrow 2 to arrow 1, drawn as a slope triangle. A DAG shows the forbidden direct path from lottery to earnings crossed out.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: compare veterans with non-veterans by OLS; biased by who enlisted voluntarily and who avoided service. Fix: instrument with lottery number. Fail: a weak instrument that barely moves the treatment makes the ratio explode; show the estimate blowing up as arrow 1 shrinks, and check first-stage strength.
real_world_anchor: Joshua Angrist (1990), 'Lifetime Earnings and the Vietnam Era Draft Lottery: Evidence from Social Security Administrative Records', American Economic Review; on weak instruments, Bound, Jaeger & Baker (1995), JASA.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: IV estimates a local average treatment effect for compliers (men whose service depended on their lottery number), not the effect for all veterans. The exclusion restriction is an assumption; for example, draft avoidance through extra schooling could violate it. Angrist found no comparable loss for nonwhite veterans.

title: Building a Fake California to Measure a Real Law
hook: To measure what California's 1988 tobacco-control law did, you would need a California that never passed it. Researchers built one: a weighted blend of other states that tracked California's cigarette sales closely for nearly two decades before the law.
core_insight: Synthetic control constructs a counterfactual as a weighted combination of untreated units that matches the treated unit's pre-treatment trajectory; the post-treatment gap estimates the effect, and placebo runs on untreated units provide inference.
key_visual: Thin gray lines for the donor states' per-capita cigarette sales. Weights flow into a handful of states (their lines thicken) and their weighted sum forms a dashed 'synthetic California' that hugs the real one before 1988, after which real California dives below it. Finally every donor state gets its own placebo synthetic; California's gap stands out from the spaghetti of placebo gaps.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: compare California with the U.S. average; the pre-trends differ, so the comparison means little. Try a single 'similar' state; poor fit. Optimize non-negative weights to match the pre-period path and covariates; tight fit. Validate with in-time placebos (fake treatment years) and in-space placebos (each donor treated as if it passed the law).
real_world_anchor: Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller (2010), 'Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California's Tobacco Control Program', JASA: by 2000, annual per-capita cigarette sales in California were about 26 packs lower than in synthetic California. Earlier: Abadie & Gardeazabal (2003) on terrorism in the Basque Country.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: A good pre-period fit is necessary but not sufficient; other post-1988 shocks could differ between California and its donors. Weights are non-negative and sum to one (no extrapolation). Check the paper's weight table before naming specific donor states on screen.

title: Why Checking Your A/B Test Early Breaks It
hook: If you check an A/B test repeatedly and stop as soon as p < 0.05, two identical versions of a website will be declared 'significantly different' far more than 5% of the time: with 20 evenly spaced looks, about a quarter of the time.
core_insight: A p-value's 5% false-positive guarantee holds for one pre-planned analysis; peeking with optional stopping gives the random walk of the test statistic many chances to cross the threshold. Sequential methods spend the error budget deliberately.
key_visual: The z-statistic as a glowing random walk drifting between horizontal boundaries at plus/minus 1.96. Hundreds of no-difference walks are released at once; any walk that touches a boundary at a check freezes red. The red fraction climbs with the number of checks (about 5%, 14%, 19%, 25%, 37% for 1, 5, 10, 20, 100 looks). Then the boundaries are reshaped into a sequential-testing funnel and the red fraction falls back to 5%.
build_fail_iterate: Run 1,000 A/A tests (no real difference) with frequent peeking; 'winners' everywhere. Fix 1: fix the sample size in advance with a power analysis and look once. Fix 2: group-sequential boundaries (alpha spending) or always-valid p-values, which allow safe early stopping; verify the 5% rate by simulation.
real_world_anchor: Armitage, McPherson & Rowe (1969), 'Repeated Significance Tests on Accumulating Data', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society A; Johari, Koomen, Pekelis & Walsh (2017), 'Peeking at A/B Tests: Why It Matters, and What to Do About It', KDD.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Inflation depends on how many looks and how they are spaced (the figures above assume equally spaced looks and a normal approximation); with unlimited peeking the false-positive rate tends toward 100%. Looking without acting is harmless; it is optional stopping that breaks the guarantee.

title: Stop Wasting Half Your Traffic on the Loser
hook: A classic A/B test keeps sending half its users to the worse option until the experiment ends. Bandit algorithms shift traffic toward the apparent winner as evidence accumulates, an idea first proposed in 1933 for clinical trials.
core_insight: The explore-exploit trade-off: Thompson sampling plays each option with the probability that it is the best given current beliefs, automatically balancing learning and earning.
key_visual: Three slot machines, each with a Beta-distribution belief curve floating above it. Every round one random draw is taken from each curve (glowing dots) and the highest dot wins the pull. Curves sharpen as data accumulate; the best machine's curve narrows and wins more and more pulls. A regret counter compares cumulative loss against a fixed 50/50 design and a greedy strategy.
build_fail_iterate: Naive greedy: always pull the current leader; it locks onto an early lucky loser. Epsilon-greedy: explores forever at a fixed rate, wasting pulls. Thompson sampling adapts. Fail: if the best option changes over time, or you need an unbiased effect estimate, bandits complicate things; add discounting or keep a fixed holdout.
real_world_anchor: William R. Thompson (1933), 'On the Likelihood That One Unknown Probability Exceeds Another in View of the Evidence of Two Samples', Biometrika; Chapelle & Li (2011), 'An Empirical Evaluation of Thompson Sampling', NeurIPS, including Yahoo! news-recommendation data.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Bandits optimize cumulative reward, not inference; adaptive allocation biases naive effect estimates. They are not always better than A/B tests: when precise effect sizes or long-term learning matter, fixed designs can be preferable.

title: How a Few Shortcuts Shrink the Whole World
hook: Take a network where everyone knows only their nearest neighbors and randomly rewire just a few percent of the links. The typical number of steps between strangers collapses, while every local neighborhood still looks just as cliquey.
core_insight: Small-world networks combine high clustering with short path lengths: a handful of random long-range ties act as shortcuts that slash typical distances without disturbing local structure.
key_visual: A ring lattice of 200 nodes, each linked to its 4 nearest neighbors. A slider rewires edges with probability p and chords fly across the circle. Two curves on a log-p axis: average path length plunging early, clustering holding high until p is large, opening the Watts-Strogatz gap. A pulse spreading from one node reaches the far side in far fewer hops once shortcuts exist.
build_fail_iterate: Build a lattice: high clustering, huge distances. Build a random graph: short distances, little clustering. Neither looks like a real social network. Rewire the lattice gradually and find the sweet spot. Then run a Milgram-style test with greedy forwarding: short paths exist, but finding them requires geographic or social cues.
real_world_anchor: Watts & Strogatz (1998), 'Collective Dynamics of Small-World Networks', Nature; Travers & Milgram (1969), Sociometry: of 296 starting letters, 64 reached the target, with about 5 intermediaries on average; Backstrom et al. (2012), 'Four Degrees of Separation', found an average distance of 4.74 hops between active Facebook users.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: 'Six degrees' overstates Milgram: most chains never completed, and completed chains may be biased toward short ones. Facebook's 4.74 is the average shortest-path length in hops (about 3.74 intermediaries); define it precisely.

title: Why Acquaintances Find You Jobs
hook: Granovetter found that people often heard about new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. Fifty years later, experiments involving about 20 million LinkedIn users tested the idea causally.
core_insight: Weak ties bridge otherwise separate clusters and carry novel information that close friends, who know what you know, cannot; in the LinkedIn experiments, moderately weak ties were the most useful for job mobility, not the weakest.
key_visual: Two dense friend clusters in different colors joined by one thin bridge edge. Information packets bounce endlessly inside each cluster and cross only via the bridge. Edge thickness encodes tie strength: removing strong edges barely changes connectivity, removing the weak bridge splits the network. An inverted-U curve of job mobility versus tie strength draws itself.
build_fail_iterate: Naive hypothesis: the strongest ties should help most. Simulate a network and propagate 'job news'; measure which ties deliver new information. Weak ties are individually less likely to help but are more numerous and more novel. Then show what a randomized recommendation experiment can identify that observational data cannot.
real_world_anchor: Mark Granovetter (1973), 'The Strength of Weak Ties', American Journal of Sociology, and Getting a Job (1974); Rajkumar et al. (2022), 'A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ties', Science: randomized variation in LinkedIn's 'People You May Know' across about 20 million people over five years.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Rajkumar et al. found an inverted U: moderately weak ties helped most and the weakest did not. Per tie, strong ties can be more helpful (Gee et al., 2017); weak ties win partly through sheer numbers.

title: Why Your Friends Have More Friends Than You
hook: On average, your friends have more friends than you do. This is a mathematical consequence of how networks are sampled, not a sign that you are unpopular.
core_insight: Reaching a person through a friendship link is biased toward popular people, who appear on many friend lists, so the average degree of friends exceeds the average degree; the bias can be exploited, for example to detect outbreaks early.
key_visual: A network with node size proportional to degree. Pick a random node: usually a small one lights up. Pick a random end of a random edge: big hubs light up again and again. Two histograms grow side by side, the degree of random people and the degree of random friends (shifted right, proportional to k p(k)). Then an epidemic ripples through and reaches the 'friend' sensors before the random ones.
build_fail_iterate: Naive surveillance: monitor a random sample of students for flu. Iterate: ask each to nominate a friend and monitor the friends instead; earlier warning. Fail: in a network where everyone has the same degree, the paradox vanishes; show it requires variation in degree (mean friend degree = mu + sigma^2/mu).
real_world_anchor: Scott Feld (1991), 'Why Your Friends Have More Friends Than You Do', American Journal of Sociology; Christakis & Fowler (2010), 'Social Network Sensors for Early Detection of Contagious Outbreaks', PLoS ONE: among Harvard students during the 2009 H1N1 flu season, the outbreak curve in nominated friends ran about two weeks ahead of that in randomly chosen students.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The paradox concerns averages; it does not mean every individual's friends are more popular. 'Mean friend degree exceeds mean degree' differs from 'most people have fewer friends than their friends' (usually also true in skewed networks, but a separate claim). The mu + sigma^2/mu formula is the mean degree of an edge-sampled node.

title: Rich-Get-Richer Networks and the Power-Law Trap
hook: If new web pages link to already-popular pages more often, a few hubs end up with an enormous share of links. But a straight line on a log-log plot, the usual 'proof' of such a power law, proves surprisingly little.
core_insight: Preferential attachment (link probability proportional to current degree) generates heavy-tailed, power-law degree distributions; but many real networks claimed to be 'scale-free' fail rigorous tests, so tails should be fitted by maximum likelihood and compared with alternatives such as the log-normal.
key_visual: A network grows node by node; each newcomer's links are drawn toward existing nodes whose glow is proportional to degree, and hubs swell. The degree histogram replots on log-log axes as a roughly straight line. Then a log-normal sample is plotted on the same axes and also looks straight over two decades, until proper likelihood fits separate the two.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: fit a line to the log-log histogram and report the slope; the estimate is biased and cannot distinguish a power law from a log-normal. Fix: maximum-likelihood estimation of the exponent above a fitted lower cutoff, a goodness-of-fit test, and likelihood-ratio comparisons against alternatives (the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman recipe).
real_world_anchor: Barabasi & Albert (1999), 'Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks', Science (with precursors in Yule 1925, Simon 1955 and Price 1976); Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), 'Power-Law Distributions in Empirical Data', SIAM Review; Broido & Clauset (2019), 'Scale-Free Networks Are Rare', Nature Communications.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Broido and Clauset's 'rare' conclusion is debated (Barabasi and others replied); present it as a challenge to over-claiming, not a final verdict. The basic Barabasi-Albert model gives a degree exponent of 3; real networks vary.

title: How the Medici Won Florence Without Being the Richest
hook: In early 15th-century Florence, the Medici were not the wealthiest family; the Strozzi were richer. Yet the Medici came to dominate the city, and a key part of the story is their position in the network of marriages and business ties.
core_insight: 'Important' has many network definitions: degree (how many ties), betweenness (how many shortest paths run through you), eigenvector centrality (ties to the well-connected). Brokers who bridge otherwise disconnected groups gain leverage that simple counts underrate.
key_visual: The Florentine elite-family marriage network laid out by force. Node sizes morph between measures: by degree, the Medici are only modestly ahead; by betweenness, the Medici balloon while others shrink, with shortest paths drawn as light streams converging through the Medici node. Remove the Medici and the network shatters into pieces.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: rank families by wealth or by number of marriage ties. Iterate: compute betweenness and reveal the Medici brokering between families that had no other connection to each other. Stress test: show how rankings shift when a single edge is removed or when the business network is used instead.
real_world_anchor: Padgett & Ansell (1993), 'Robust Action and the Rise of the Medici, 1400-1434', American Journal of Sociology; the marriage network of 16 elite families (from Breiger & Pattison, 1986) is a standard small dataset, included for example in NetworkX.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: In the standard marriage network the Medici also have the highest degree (6), but their lead in betweenness is far larger; say this accurately. Padgett and Ansell's argument combines marriage networks, economic networks and historical context; centrality is part of the story, not a complete explanation.

title: The Random Surfer Behind Google
hook: Google's original ranking idea can be described as a bored web surfer clicking random links forever. The fraction of time that surfer spends on each page is its PageRank.
core_insight: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a Markov chain on the link graph with random teleportation, equivalently the leading eigenvector of the 'Google matrix': a page matters if pages that matter link to it.
key_visual: A directed graph of about 12 pages. A glowing token hops along the arrows while a counter on each node tallies visits and node size tracks share of time. In parallel, 'probability paint' flows along edges each iteration until the colors stop changing (power iteration converging to the eigenvector). Then a dead-end page and a two-page trap appear and the token gets stuck, until teleportation beams fire 15% of the time and rescue it.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: rank pages by number of incoming links; easily gamed by link farms. Fix 1: weight each link by the linker's own rank (a recursive definition). Fail: dead ends and link traps soak up all the rank. Fix 2: teleport with probability 1 - d (d = 0.85). Remaining weakness: link spam still has some effect, which is why real search engines use many signals.
real_world_anchor: Brin & Page (1998), 'The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine', Computer Networks and ISDN Systems; Page, Brin, Motwani & Winograd (1999), 'The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web'; related ideas include Pinski & Narin (1976) on citation influence and Kleinberg's HITS (1999).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Modern search ranking uses many signals beyond PageRank; do not imply PageRank alone runs search today. The damping factor 0.85 is the commonly cited value from the original papers, not a law.

title: The Karate Club That Split in Two
hook: In the 1970s an anthropologist mapped the friendships in a university karate club just before a dispute split it in two. Algorithms given only the friendship links can predict who ended up on which side for all but one member.
core_insight: Community detection finds groups with more internal than external ties (for example by maximizing modularity); but algorithms will also 'find' communities in purely random networks, so detected structure must be compared with a null model.
key_visual: Zachary's 34-member network. The edges with the highest betweenness glow and are snipped one by one (Girvan-Newman); the network falls apart into two halves that recolor to match the real post-split factions, with a single mismatch. Then a random graph with the same degrees goes through modularity maximization and also yields 'communities' with clearly positive modularity.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: run k-means on the rows of the adjacency matrix; poor. Girvan-Newman edge betweenness: nearly perfect on the karate club. Fail 1: modularity finds 'communities' in random graphs. Fail 2: the resolution limit merges small genuine communities in large networks. Fix: compare against null models and check results across methods and resolutions.
real_world_anchor: Wayne Zachary (1977), 'An Information Flow Model for Conflict and Fission in Small Groups', Journal of Anthropological Research; Girvan & Newman (2002), PNAS; Guimera, Sales-Pardo & Amaral (2004), Physical Review E, on modularity in random graphs; Fortunato & Barthelemy (2007), PNAS, on the resolution limit.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Girvan-Newman misclassified one member (node 3 in the usual labeling); do not say 'perfectly'. The real factions are one plausible partition among several; detected communities are always relative to a model.

title: Did Your Friends Make You Do It?
hook: Obesity, smoking and happiness appear to 'spread' through social networks. But people also choose friends who resemble them, and in observational network data those two explanations can be impossible to tell apart.
core_insight: Homophily (similar people connect) and contagion (connected people become similar) produce the same correlations between friends; without experiments or strong assumptions, observational network data cannot separate influence from selection.
key_visual: Two side-by-side worlds start from the same scattered, colored nodes. World A (homophily): colors stay fixed while edges rewire toward same-colored nodes. World B (contagion): edges stay fixed while nodes repaint to match their neighbors. Both converge to visually identical snapshots of clustered colors. A third world adds a hidden trait driving both, revealed at the end as an invisible field.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: regress each person's change on friends' earlier states and call it influence. Simulate pure homophily on a hidden trait; the naive estimator reports 'contagion'. Fix: randomized experiments that assign exposure, or matched-sample methods that account for observed homophily, which substantially shrink estimated influence.
real_world_anchor: Christakis & Fowler (2007), 'The Spread of Obesity in a Large Social Network over 32 Years', New England Journal of Medicine (Framingham Heart Study); Shalizi & Thomas (2011), 'Homophily and Contagion Are Generically Confounded in Observational Social Network Studies', Sociological Methods & Research; Aral, Muchnik & Sundararajan (2009), PNAS: homophily explained more than half of the apparent contagion in adoption of a mobile service.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Shalizi and Thomas show non-identifiability without further assumptions, not that contagion never happens. Christakis and Fowler's findings are contested, not disproven; frame this as a methodological debate.

title: When Your Control Group Catches the Treatment
hook: Randomly give half of a social network's users a new feature and the 'control' half still feels it, through friends who have it. The experiment's comparison can then be biased in either direction.
core_insight: Standard experiments assume one unit's treatment does not affect another's outcome (SUTVA). In networks and marketplaces spillovers violate this, so you randomize clusters of connected units to capture the total effect.
key_visual: A social network with treated nodes in gold and controls in gray. Effects ripple out from gold nodes along edges and tint neighboring gray nodes, so the control group warms up and the measured difference shrinks. Then the network is partitioned into clusters (graph cluster randomization): whole clusters flip gold together and spillover across cluster boundaries is minimal.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: randomize individuals on a simulated network with a known global effect; the estimate is badly biased. Fix: cluster randomization; closer to the truth but noisier, because there are fewer effective units. Tune cluster size to trade bias against variance. Contrast with a marketplace, where treated buyers take goods from controls and bias runs the other way.
real_world_anchor: Ugander, Karrer, Backstrom & Kleinberg (2013), 'Graph Cluster Randomization: Network Exposure to Multiple Universes', KDD; SUTVA formalized by Donald Rubin (1980); Blake & Coey (2014) documented test-control interference in eBay marketplace experiments.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Interference can bias estimates upward (marketplace cannibalization) or downward (positive spillovers to controls); say both. Cluster randomization reduces spillover but rarely eliminates it.

title: Why Epidemics Overshoot Herd Immunity
hook: An unchecked epidemic does not stop when it reaches herd immunity; it keeps going. In the simplest model with R0 = 2.5, the number of people currently infected peaks once 60% have caught it, yet about 89% are eventually infected.
core_insight: In SIR dynamics, the number currently infected peaks when the susceptible fraction falls to 1/R0 (the herd-immunity threshold), but the many people still infectious at that moment keep transmitting, so the epidemic overshoots. R0 above or below 1 is a sharp threshold.
key_visual: A box of bouncing dots (susceptible blue, infected red, recovered gray) next to a phase plane with S on the x-axis and I on the y-axis. The trajectory arcs up, peaks exactly as S crosses the dashed line at 1/R0, then curves down while S keeps sliding left, ending far past the line. A slider varies R0: below 1 the arc never rises; above 1 it overshoots.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: pure exponential growth, which predicts infections rising forever. Fix: deplete susceptibles (SIR). Fail: homogeneous mixing overestimates spread compared with a heterogeneous contact network, where the threshold is also lower. Compare SIR on a network with the well-mixed version, and fit the classic boarding-school outbreak data.
real_world_anchor: Kermack & McKendrick (1927), 'A Contribution to the Mathematical Theory of Epidemics', Proceedings of the Royal Society A; classic dataset: influenza at an English boys' boarding school (BMJ, 1978), where 512 of 763 boys were confined to bed and the outbreak is well fitted by SIR.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The 89% and 60% figures assume homogeneous mixing, no interventions and lasting immunity; real epidemics are shaped by behavior and heterogeneity. The herd-immunity threshold 1 - 1/R0 is where growth stops, not where the epidemic ends.

title: Why Behaviors Don't Spread Like Viruses
hook: Random long-range ties make diseases and rumors spread faster. But in an online experiment, a health behavior spread farther and faster through clustered networks, because people needed to hear about it from several contacts.
core_insight: Simple contagions need one contact; complex contagions need reinforcement from several. Clustering supplies redundant exposures, so the network that is best for spreading a virus can be worst for spreading a costly behavior.
key_visual: Two networks with identical numbers of nodes and edges, a clustered lattice and a randomly rewired version. A simple contagion (one exposure needed) is released in both and the random network wins the race. Then a complex contagion (two exposures needed): it stalls in the random network, where single long ties cannot deliver double exposure, but marches across the lattice in a widening front.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: assume more shortcuts means faster spread for everything. Run a two-exposure contagion on increasingly rewired small-world networks; the most randomized ones fail. Iterate: measure 'wide bridges' (several parallel ties between clusters) and show that they carry complex contagions.
real_world_anchor: Centola & Macy (2007), 'Complex Contagions and the Weakness of Long Ties', American Journal of Sociology; Damon Centola (2010), 'The Spread of Behavior in an Online Social Network Experiment', Science: sign-ups for a health forum spread farther and faster in clustered networks than in random ones.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Complex contagion does not refute the strength of weak ties for information; it specifies when long ties fail. Centola's experiment used anonymous 'health buddies' in designed networks, so generalizing to organic networks is an inference.

title: Two Nearly Identical Crowds: One Riots, One Doesn't
hook: Imagine 100 people whose riot thresholds are 0, 1, 2, ... 99 (each joins once that many others already have): everyone ends up rioting. Change one person's threshold from 1 to 2 and only one person riots.
core_insight: Collective outcomes depend on the whole distribution of individual thresholds, not on average dispositions; tiny changes to that distribution can switch a cascade on or off, so you cannot read a crowd's character from its behavior.
key_visual: 100 figures in a row ordered by threshold, each with a number above its head. The zero-threshold instigator lights up, triggering the 1, then the 2, a domino wave across all 100. Rewind, change one '1' to a '2', and the instigator lights up alone. A cumulative-distribution plot with the 45-degree line shows the equilibria as crossing points.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: predict rioting from the average threshold; both crowds have nearly identical averages but opposite outcomes. Fix: use the cumulative threshold distribution and find where it first meets y = x. Extend to networks, where people respond to the neighbors they can see rather than the whole crowd.
real_world_anchor: Mark Granovetter (1978), 'Threshold Models of Collective Behavior', American Journal of Sociology.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: This is a stylized model, not evidence about specific real riots. Granovetter's point is that observers would describe the two crowds very differently despite near-identical individuals.

title: How Rational People Join the Wrong Crowd
hook: A line of perfectly rational people can all make the same wrong choice, each correctly reasoning that the people before them probably knew something. After just two matching choices, private information can stop mattering.
core_insight: When people see others' actions but not their private information, an early run of matching choices can make ignoring one's own signal rational; the resulting cascade aggregates almost nothing, so it can be wrong and fragile.
key_visual: Two urns: A holds 2 red and 1 blue, B holds 1 red and 2 blue. People queue; each privately draws a ball (shown only in their thought bubble) and publicly announces 'A' or 'B', while a belief meter above the queue updates. After two 'A' announcements, the third person draws blue yet announces 'A'; their bubble grays out and everyone after follows. The true urn is revealed: B.
build_fail_iterate: Simulate 1,000 queues and count how often the crowd ends up wrong even though most private draws pointed the right way. Fix: make choices reveal signals (people announce their draws) and accuracy soars. Show fragility: one credible public piece of contrary information can break a cascade.
real_world_anchor: Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer & Welch (1992), 'A Theory of Fads, Fashion, Custom, and Cultural Change as Informational Cascades', Journal of Political Economy; Anderson & Holt (1997), 'Information Cascades in the Laboratory', American Economic Review.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: These cascades arise among fully rational agents; no conformity pressure is needed, so distinguish them from Asch-style conformity. In the lab cascades formed often but not always; some participants followed their own signals.

title: The Math Behind the Wisdom of Crowds
hook: At a 1906 livestock fair, about 800 people guessed the weight of an ox, and the middle guess (1,207 lb) was within 1% of the true dressed weight (1,198 lb). Let a crowd see each other's guesses, though, and the magic can evaporate.
core_insight: Crowd error = average individual error minus the diversity of the guesses (the diversity prediction theorem). Crowds are wise when errors are independent and diverse; social influence that shrinks diversity can undermine the effect.
key_visual: Guesses as dots on a number line with the true value as a gold pin. Each dot's squared error is drawn as a square; the crowd mean's squared error is one small square. A geometric decomposition shows: average square area = the crowd's square + the spread around the mean. Then social influence pulls the dots together; the spread term shrinks while the crowd's mean drifts off target.
build_fail_iterate: Simulate independent noisy guessers; the crowd beats nearly everyone. Add a shared bias; no amount of averaging fixes it. Add social influence (people see the running average); diversity collapses and confidence rises without accuracy improving. Fix: collect independent estimates before discussion, and use the median when guesses are heavy-tailed.
real_world_anchor: Francis Galton (1907), 'Vox Populi', Nature: 787 legible guesses from the West of England Fat Stock and Poultry Exhibition in Plymouth; Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer & Helbing (2011), 'How Social Influence Can Undermine the Wisdom of Crowd Effect', PNAS; the diversity prediction theorem is from Scott Page, The Difference (2007).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Galton reported the median (1,207 lb); the often-quoted mean of about 1,197 lb was calculated separately. The theorem is an identity about squared error of the mean; it does not guarantee crowds beat experts.

title: Rewind the World: Would the Same Song Be a Hit?
hook: In an online experiment with over 14,000 participants, researchers created eight parallel 'worlds' of the same music market. The same song could become a hit in one world and a flop in another.
core_insight: Social influence makes success both more unequal and more unpredictable: small early random advantages get amplified, so quality only loosely constrains outcomes.
key_visual: Nine parallel panels (eight social-influence worlds plus one independent world), each a bar-chart race of 48 songs' download counts, all starting at zero. In the influence worlds early random leads balloon into dominance, with different winners in different panels; the independent world stays flatter. A closing scatter plots quality (independent-world rank) against success, with a widening funnel of outcomes for mid-quality songs.
build_fail_iterate: Build a naive market where people choose purely on song quality; outcomes are predictable and inequality is modest. Add visible download counts; inequality and unpredictability explode. Turn the influence strength up and down to show both rising together, foreshadowing the Polya urn of episode 80.
real_world_anchor: Salganik, Dodds & Watts (2006), 'Experimental Study of Inequality and Unpredictability in an Artificial Cultural Market', Science: 14,341 participants, 48 songs by unknown bands, eight social-influence worlds plus an independent condition.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Quality still mattered: the best songs rarely did very badly and the worst rarely did very well; do not say success is 'pure luck'. Participants were mostly young internet users recruited online, so applying the result to real markets is an inference.

title: How Open-Minded People Split Into Camps
hook: Give a population a simple, reasonable rule (average your opinion with everyone who is not too far from you) and instead of reaching consensus it can freeze into permanent, separate camps.
core_insight: In bounded-confidence models agents listen only to opinions within a tolerance epsilon; small epsilon yields several stable clusters (roughly 1/(2 epsilon) of them), larger epsilon yields consensus, so fragmentation can emerge without stubbornness or extremists.
key_visual: The iconic Hegselmann-Krause braid: 100 opinions as glowing threads moving over time on a vertical axis from 0 to 1. Threads merge into rivers; with small epsilon several rivers form and never meet. A slider sweeps epsilon and the number of rivers drops in steps until a single consensus line remains. A side panel shows the classic DeGroot model, where everyone listens to everyone, always converging.
build_fail_iterate: Start with DeGroot averaging: everyone converges, which is unrealistic. Add bounded confidence: clusters form. Add a few stubborn extremists: they drag clusters apart into polarized camps. Measure cluster count against epsilon and compare with the 1/(2 epsilon) rule of thumb.
real_world_anchor: Hegselmann & Krause (2002), 'Opinion Dynamics and Bounded Confidence: Models, Analysis and Simulation', Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation; Deffuant, Neau, Amblard & Weisbuch (2000), Advances in Complex Systems; Morris DeGroot (1974), 'Reaching a Consensus', JASA.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The 1/(2 epsilon) rule is approximate and was noted for the Deffuant model with uniformly spread initial opinions. These are theoretical models; direct empirical validation of bounded confidence is limited.

title: Breaking the Echo Chamber Can Backfire
hook: An intuitive fix for polarization is to expose people to the other side. When researchers paid Twitter users to follow a bot sharing opposing political views for a month, Republicans became more conservative, not less.
core_insight: Exposure to opposing views is not automatically moderating; identity and how content is encountered matter, so well-intended interventions need experimental testing rather than intuition.
key_visual: Opinion distributions as two hills on a horizontal axis. A stream of 'opposing' message particles is aimed at one hill: in the naive model the hill drifts toward the center; in the observed result it recoils outward. Before and after violin shapes with confidence intervals show the measured shift for Republicans (significant) and Democrats (small, not significant).
build_fail_iterate: Build a naive opinion model where exposure pulls opinions together; polarization vanishes in simulation. Contrast it with the field experiment. Revise the model with a backfire response to out-group sources and show that the outcome hinges on the mechanism, which is exactly why you run the experiment.
real_world_anchor: Bail et al. (2018), 'Exposure to Opposing Views on Social Media Can Increase Political Polarization', PNAS: Twitter users were paid to follow a bot that retweeted elected officials and opinion leaders from the opposing party for one month.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Democrats' shift toward more liberal views was not statistically significant; report only the Republican result as significant. Later large studies (e.g. the 2023 Meta-academic collaborations in Science and Nature) found that changing feeds had little short-term effect on polarization; do not generalize to 'exposure always backfires'.

title: Mild Preferences, Extreme Segregation
hook: Suppose everyone is content to be in the minority, happy as long as at least a third of their neighbors are like them. A city of such people can still end up sharply segregated.
core_insight: In Schelling's model, individually mild preferences produce strongly segregated patterns through chain reactions of moves: macro patterns do not reveal micro motives.
key_visual: A 50 x 50 grid of two colors of tiles with some empty cells, starting as salt-and-pepper noise. Unhappy tiles (fewer than a third of neighbors alike) pulse and hop to random empty cells. Within a few rounds, large single-color regions crystallize. A meter shows the average share of same-color neighbors climbing from about 50% to about 75%, while the preference line stays fixed at 33%.
build_fail_iterate: Naive expectation: a tolerance of one third gives a mixed city. Run it; segregation. Iterate: sweep the threshold to find the tipping region; give agents a taste for diversity (also unhappy if too surrounded by their own kind) and watch segregation persist. Close with what the model cannot tell you about real cities.
real_world_anchor: Thomas Schelling (1971), 'Dynamic Models of Segregation', Journal of Mathematical Sociology, originally worked out by hand with coins on a checkerboard; Schelling shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Economics.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The model shows mild preferences are sufficient to produce segregation, not that real segregation is caused by them; discriminatory policies such as redlining and housing discrimination are well documented. Exact segregation levels depend on neighborhood definition, density and movement rules.

title: The Winning Strategy That Never Won a Single Game
hook: In Robert Axelrod's famous tournaments of computer programs playing the repeated prisoner's dilemma, the winner was the simplest entry, and it never outscored any single opponent it played.
core_insight: Tit for Tat (cooperate first, then copy your partner's last move) wins by eliciting cooperation, not by beating anyone: being nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear pays when interactions repeat.
key_visual: A round-robin matrix of strategies drawn as procedural icons, each cell filling with a match score as games play out. Tit for Tat never takes the larger share in any single match, yet its row total is the highest. Then an evolutionary view: strategy populations as colored bands whose widths change over generations; exploiters boom, then crash as their prey disappears, while Tit for Tat spreads.
build_fail_iterate: Enter Always Defect: it wins or ties every head-to-head match but scores poorly overall. Enter Always Cooperate: exploited. Tit for Tat: wins. Fail: add noise (occasional mistaken moves) and two Tit for Tat players fall into endless retaliation. Fix: Generous Tit for Tat or Win-Stay, Lose-Shift.
real_world_anchor: Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments (results published in the Journal of Conflict Resolution, 1980) and The Evolution of Cooperation (1984); Axelrod & Hamilton (1981), Science. Tit for Tat was submitted by Anatol Rapoport and won both tournaments.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Tit for Tat is not the best strategy in every environment; its success depended on the field of entries, and under noise more forgiving strategies do better (Nowak & Sigmund, 1992 and 1993). 'Never outscored an opponent' means within each match it at best tied its partner.

title: The Tragedy of the Commons Isn't Inevitable
hook: The 'tragedy of the commons' says shared resources are doomed to be overused. Yet a Swiss alpine village has governed its shared pastures under community rules for centuries, and the political scientist who documented such cases won a Nobel Prize.
core_insight: Open-access resources collapse in simple models, but communities can sustain commons through monitoring, graduated sanctions and locally made rules; in experiments, the option to punish free-riders makes cooperation stable.
key_visual: A circular pasture whose grass regrows logistically while herder agents add cows whenever their private gain exceeds their share of the damage; the grass fades to bare earth as cow counts spike. Then a public-goods game view: contributions per round step downward without punishment, but climb and stabilize once punishment is enabled, shown as two line traces.
build_fail_iterate: Build Hardin's model: collapse. Fix attempt 1: rely on goodwill (a few unconditional cooperators); they are exploited and collapse continues. Fix 2: add monitoring and costly punishment; cooperation stabilizes. Fail: if punishment is too costly or aimed at cooperators ('antisocial punishment'), outcomes degrade; institutional design matters.
real_world_anchor: Garrett Hardin (1968), 'The Tragedy of the Commons', Science; Elinor Ostrom (1990), Governing the Commons, including Torbel, Switzerland, whose communal grazing rules date to 1517 (Ostrom shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Economics); Fehr & Gachter (2000), 'Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments', American Economic Review.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Hardin described unmanaged open access; Ostrom showed commons are often successfully managed, not that tragedies never happen (fishery collapses are real). Antisocial punishment varies a lot across societies (Herrmann, Thoni & Gachter, 2008).

title: Two Countries, Same Inequality Score, Different Worlds
hook: Two societies can have exactly the same Gini coefficient while one has a struggling bottom and the other a runaway top. When Lorenz curves cross, a single number cannot rank inequality.
core_insight: The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income held by the poorest x% of people; the Gini coefficient is twice the area between it and the line of perfect equality. Different shapes can enclose the same area, so the Gini hides where inequality lives.
key_visual: People as bars sorted from poorest to richest; their incomes stack into a cumulative curve bowing below the 45-degree equality line, and the area between them fills with color and converts into a Gini readout. A second curve morphs in and crosses the first, sagging more at the bottom and less at the top, while the Gini counter stays exactly the same.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: rank countries by Gini alone. Construct two income distributions with equal Gini but opposite policy implications. Iterate: compare the top 1% share, the Palma ratio and the Atkinson index at different levels of inequality aversion, and show how they disagree in principled ways.
real_world_anchor: Max O. Lorenz (1905), 'Methods of Measuring the Concentration of Wealth', Publications of the American Statistical Association; Corrado Gini (1912); Anthony Atkinson (1970), 'On the Measurement of Inequality', Journal of Economic Theory, showing that when Lorenz curves cross, any ranking embodies a value judgment.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Gini values depend on the income definition (before or after taxes and transfers, household or individual, income or consumption); compare like with like. With non-negative incomes the Gini lies between 0 and 1; negative wealth can push it above 1.

title: Fair Coin Flips, Wildly Unfair Outcomes
hook: Simulate an economy where every trade is a fair coin flip and the stake is a fraction of the poorer trader's wealth. Nobody cheats and nobody has an edge, yet wealth concentrates into fewer and fewer hands.
core_insight: Repeated fair multiplicative bets are not fair over time: losses compound more than gains (lose 20% then gain 20% and you are at 96%), so chance plus proportional stakes drives wealth toward concentration unless something redistributes.
key_visual: A room of 500 agents as columns of gold coins. Random pairs meet, a coin flips, and a slice of the poorer agent's stack moves across. Columns jitter, then a few towers rise while most shrink. The wealth histogram skews, the Lorenz curve from episode 78 sags toward the corner, and a Gini meter climbs. A redistribution slider (a small tax shared equally) halts the climb at a finite Gini.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: fair bets of a fixed dollar amount; wealth spreads into an exponential-like distribution but does not fully concentrate. Switch to stakes proportional to the poorer trader's wealth; wealth condenses. Add a small redistributive tax; a stable but unequal distribution emerges. Plot the long-run Gini against the tax rate.
real_world_anchor: Anirban Chakraborti (2002), 'Distributions of Money in Model Markets of Economy', International Journal of Modern Physics C; Brian Hayes (2002), 'Follow the Money', American Scientist, which named the 'yard-sale model'; Bruce Boghosian (2019), 'Is Inequality Inevitable?', Scientific American. Related: Epstein & Axtell's Sugarscape in Growing Artificial Societies (1996).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: This is a toy model: it shows chance alone can generate extreme inequality, not that real inequality is purely chance. Complete concentration is a long-run limit of the pure model.

title: Why Early Luck Gets Locked In
hook: Start an urn with one red and one blue ball, then repeatedly draw a ball and return it along with another of the same color. The red fraction settles down, but to a random value, and every value between 0 and 1 is equally likely.
core_insight: Cumulative advantage (the Matthew effect) makes outcomes path-dependent: early random draws are amplified and then frozen in, so identical starting points lead to very different stable endpoints.
key_visual: Ten urns side by side filling with balls. Each urn's red-fraction trace wobbles wildly at first and then flattens, at ten different heights. Thousands of runs pile their final fractions into a histogram that comes out flat from 0 to 1. Then a schematic of a 'success breeds success' field experiment: randomly boosted projects pull ahead of matched controls.
build_fail_iterate: Naive expectation: a fair start means 50/50 in the long run. Simulate: the fractions do converge, but each run to a different value. Start with 10 balls of each color and outcomes become far more stable. Then give one color a small quality edge and show how luck and merit mix.
real_world_anchor: Eggenberger & Polya (1923) introduced the urn model; Robert K. Merton (1968), 'The Matthew Effect in Science', Science; van de Rijt, Kang, Restivo & Patil (2014), 'Field Experiments of Success-Breeds-Success Dynamics', PNAS: randomly granting early success (e.g. Kickstarter funding, Wikipedia awards) increased later success.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The uniform limit holds specifically for a one-red, one-blue start with one ball added per draw; other starts give Beta distributions. van de Rijt et al. found diminishing returns to larger initial boosts.

title: Why 'The' Is Twice as Common as 'Of'
hook: In a classic million-word corpus of American English, 'the' makes up about 7% of all words and 'of' about 3.5%, roughly half as much. Frequency keeps falling roughly as 1/rank for thousands of words.
core_insight: Word frequency is roughly inversely proportional to rank (Zipf's law): a handful of words dominate any text while most words are rare, with big consequences for text analysis. But random typing also produces Zipf-like curves, so the curve alone says little about mechanisms.
key_visual: Words as stacked tiles from the tallest ('the') to a long tail of tiny ones. The axes switch to log-log and the jagged staircase straightens into a line of slope about -1. Then a monkey at a typewriter generates random letters and spaces; its 'word' frequencies, plotted the same way, also form a near-straight line.
build_fail_iterate: Naive inference: Zipf's law proves a universal principle of least effort. Test it: random typing reproduces a Zipf-like curve. Iterate: compare goodness of fit and the bends at the head and tail, and argue that claims about mechanism need more than the curve (linking back to episode 61's power-law caution).
real_world_anchor: George Kingsley Zipf, Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort (1949); Brown Corpus counts from Kucera & Francis (1967) ('the' about 69,971 times and 'of' about 36,411 times in roughly one million words); George Miller (1957) and Wentian Li (1992), IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, on Zipf-like laws in random text.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Zipf's law is an approximation; the head and tail deviate and exponents vary by corpus and language. Random-text curves differ from real language in detail; the point is only that the curve alone is not proof of a mechanism.

title: The Boring Words That Unmasked an Author
hook: Twelve of the Federalist Papers were claimed by both Alexander Hamilton and James Madison. Statisticians settled it in the 1960s using not ideas or rhetoric but humble words like 'upon', which Hamilton used far more often than Madison.
core_insight: Bag of words: represent a document by its word counts and ignore order. Function words are used habitually and unconsciously, so their rates act as an authorial fingerprint that a probabilistic model can exploit.
key_visual: Each paper becomes a point in a space of function-word rates ('upon', 'whilst', 'by', 'to'). Hamilton's known papers form a red cluster and Madison's a blue cluster. The 12 disputed papers fly in one by one and land near Madison's cluster. A bar chart of 'upon' per 1,000 words: about 3 for Hamilton, about 0.2 for Madison.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: use content words such as 'war' or 'states'; they track the topic, not the author, and mislead. Iterate: restrict to function words, model their counts with Poisson or negative binomial distributions, and compute Bayesian odds for each disputed paper. Validate first on papers of known authorship.
real_world_anchor: Mosteller & Wallace (1963), 'Inference in an Authorship Problem', JASA, and Inference and Disputed Authorship: The Federalist (1964), concluding Madison very likely wrote all 12 disputed papers.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Bag of words ignores order and meaning; it works here because the task is stylistic. Historians (notably Douglass Adair, 1944) had already argued for Madison; the statistics strengthened that case rather than overturning a consensus.

title: The Most Common Words Tell You the Least
hook: Ask a computer which words best describe a speech and raw counts answer 'the', 'and', 'of'. The words that actually distinguish a document are the ones it uses much more than everyone else.
core_insight: Distinctiveness is frequency relative to a baseline: TF-IDF down-weights words that appear in many documents, and for comparing groups, regularized log-odds handle the opposite failure, where rare words look falsely extreme.
key_visual: A bar chart of a speech's words sorted by count; each bar is multiplied by its IDF weight, the 'the/and/of' bars sink into the floor and distinctive terms rise. Then a 'fightin' words' scatter: x = word frequency, y = party log-odds; naive log-odds fling rare words to the extremes in a funnel, while the regularized version calms them.
build_fail_iterate: Naive 1: raw counts; stop words dominate. Naive 2: delete a stop-word list; generic common words still dominate. Naive 3: difference in proportions between groups; common words dominate. Naive 4: log-odds ratio; rare words dominate. Fix: TF-IDF for describing documents, and log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior for contrasting groups.
real_world_anchor: Karen Sparck Jones (1972), 'A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval', Journal of Documentation (inverse document frequency); Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn (2008), 'Fightin' Words: Lexical Feature Selection and Evaluation for Identifying the Content of Political Conflict', Political Analysis.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: TF-IDF has many variants (log scaling, smoothing); state which one is shown. Distinctive words are associations, not evidence of what a group believes; context matters.

title: An Algorithm That Finds Topics Without Reading
hook: A topic model knows nothing about what words mean, yet it can sort thousands of documents into coherent themes. Strangely, the version that best predicts held-out text is not necessarily the one humans find most interpretable.
core_insight: Latent Dirichlet Allocation treats each document as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words; topics are statistical co-occurrence patterns, and their number and labels are human choices.
key_visual: Documents as jars of colored word-marbles. The model explains each jar as a recipe mixing a few 'topic jars'; iteration by iteration (Gibbs sampling) marbles recolor by topic until the topic jars become coherent, e.g. {tax, budget, spending} versus {troops, war, security}. A slider for the number of topics K splits and merges topics live.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: cluster documents with k-means on word counts, forcing each document into exactly one cluster. Fix: mixed membership via LDA. Fail: choose K purely by held-out likelihood and interpretability suffers. Iterate: add coherence measures, human validation (word-intrusion tests) and multiple random seeds, and report how stable the topics are.
real_world_anchor: Blei, Ng & Jordan (2003), 'Latent Dirichlet Allocation', Journal of Machine Learning Research; Chang et al. (2009), 'Reading Tea Leaves: How Humans Interpret Topic Models', NeurIPS: held-out likelihood did not track human interpretability and sometimes moved in the opposite direction; Quinn et al. (2010), American Journal of Political Science, applied topic models to U.S. Senate speeches.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Topic labels are researchers' interpretations; present them as such. Results vary with random seed, preprocessing and K.

title: King - Man + Woman = Queen? Not Quite
hook: Word vectors famously solve 'king - man + woman = queen'. Less famously, the standard demo excludes the input words from the answer; without that rule, the nearest vector is often just 'king' again.
core_insight: Embeddings place words in a space where closeness reflects shared contexts ('you shall know a word by the company it keeps'); relationships appear as approximate directions, but analogy arithmetic is noisier than the demos suggest.
key_visual: Words as glowing points in 3-D (a projection of a high-dimensional space). A context window slides over sentences, nudging co-occurring words toward each other. Then a parallelogram: king-to-queen parallel to man-to-woman, with the result vector landing in a neighborhood containing both 'queen' and 'king', and the demo's exclusion rule shown as a hand blocking 'king'.
build_fail_iterate: Naive representation: one-hot vectors, where every word is equally far from every other. Iterate: raw co-occurrence counts, which are huge and dominated by frequent words. Fix: compress into dense vectors (SVD or word2vec). Then test analogies honestly, with and without excluding the input words, and report accuracy.
real_world_anchor: Mikolov et al. (2013), 'Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space' (word2vec); J. R. Firth (1957) on the distributional hypothesis; Nissim, van Noord & van der Goot (2020), 'Fair Is Better than Sensational: Man Is to Doctor as Woman Is to Doctor', Computational Linguistics.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The analogy holds only approximately, in some embeddings, and with the exclusion rule; never imply exact equality. Embedding geometry depends on the corpus and training settings; meanings are relational, not definitions.

title: Word Vectors as a Telescope on Culture
hook: Word embeddings trained on a century of American text place occupations nearer 'woman' or 'man' in ways that track the actual share of women in those jobs in census data. The 'bias' is also a measurement.
core_insight: Embeddings absorb the associations in their training text, stereotypes included. That is a problem when they are deployed in products and an opportunity for social science: projecting words onto axes such as man-woman or rich-poor measures cultural associations and how they change.
key_visual: An axis drawn from 'man' to 'woman' through embedding space, with occupation words casting perpendicular shadows onto it. A decade slider (1910 to 1990) moves the occupations along the axis while the census share of women in each job animates beside them, the two moving together. A second axis, rich minus poor, shows words like 'opera', 'golf' and 'camping' sliding along it.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: treat embeddings as neutral 'meaning'. Test them with association tests (an IAT for word vectors); they reproduce known human biases. Attempted fix: 'debias' by projecting out a gender direction; the bias remains recoverable from word neighborhoods. Flip the lens: use the associations deliberately as a measurement instrument, with validation.
real_world_anchor: Caliskan, Bryson & Narayanan (2017), 'Semantics Derived Automatically from Language Corpora Contain Human-Like Biases', Science; Garg, Schiebinger, Jurafsky & Zou (2018), 'Word Embeddings Quantify 100 Years of Gender and Ethnic Stereotypes', PNAS; Kozlowski, Taddy & Evans (2019), 'The Geometry of Culture', American Sociological Review; Gonen & Goldberg (2019) on the limits of debiasing.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Embedding associations reflect the corpus (books, news), not directly what the population believes. The well-known Bolukbasi et al. (2016) 'computer programmer : homemaker' analogy depended on how analogy search was constrained; cite it with that caveat.

title: Why Your Sentiment Analyzer Hates Accountants
hook: A widely used general-purpose dictionary labels words like 'tax', 'cost', 'capital' and 'liability' as negative. In corporate annual reports, almost three-quarters of the words it flags as negative are not negative in that context.
core_insight: Sentiment measurement is domain-specific: dictionaries and models built for one context misread another, and negation, sarcasm and topic get confused with tone. Validate against human-coded samples from your own domain.
key_visual: Text flows through a 'sentiment filter' that colors words red or green. On a financial report, red floods the screen ('liability', 'tax', 'depreciation'). A split screen with a finance-specific dictionary shows the red receding to genuinely negative terms ('loss', 'impairment'). Then negation: 'not bad' scores negative under word counting until a parsing step flips it.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: count positive minus negative words with a general dictionary; financial documents look gloomy for no reason. Fix 1: a domain-specific word list. Fail: negation and sarcasm. Fix 2: supervised models trained on hand-labeled examples from the domain, with agreement against human coders always reported.
real_world_anchor: Loughran & McDonald (2011), 'When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10-Ks', Journal of Finance: almost three-fourths of the words classified as negative by the Harvard General Inquirer dictionary were typically not negative in financial contexts.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The three-quarters figure comes from Loughran and McDonald's 10-K sample, not from sentiment tasks in general. Modern LLM-based classifiers also need validation in each domain; they reduce but do not remove the problem.

title: Can an AI Replace a Survey of Real People?
hook: Prompt a language model with the demographic backstory of a real survey respondent and it can reproduce many groups' average voting patterns surprisingly well. But using it as a replacement fails in quieter ways: answers are too uniform and shift with prompt wording.
core_insight: LLM 'silicon samples' can mirror group-level associations in their training data (algorithmic fidelity), but they compress variance, are sensitive to prompts and model versions, and cannot be assumed representative; they suit pilots and hypothesis generation, not substitution for measurement.
key_visual: Two histograms grow side by side for the same survey question: real respondents (wide, lumpy) and silicon respondents (narrow, peaked), with means close but spreads very different. A dial labeled 'prompt wording' turns and the silicon histogram jumps while the human one does not. A KL-divergence meter (episode 8) quantifies the mismatch.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: ask the model 'What do Americans think about X?'; it gives one stereotyped answer. Iterate: condition on individual backstories; group means improve. Fail: compare full distributions and repeat months later; variance is too low and results drift across model versions. Fix: use silicon samples to generate hypotheses and validate every use against fresh human data.
real_world_anchor: Argyle et al. (2023), 'Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples', Political Analysis (GPT-3 conditioned on American National Election Studies backstories); Bisbee et al. (2024), 'Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data? The Perils of Large Language Models', Political Analysis; Santurkar et al. (2023), 'Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?', ICML.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Findings are specific to particular models and dates; newer models may behave differently, so avoid absolute claims. 'Algorithmic fidelity' means matching conditional patterns in human responses; it says nothing about the model holding opinions.

title: Why 250,000 Survey Responses Were Worth Fewer Than 10
hook: In 2021, a COVID survey collecting about 250,000 responses a week overestimated U.S. vaccine uptake by 17 percentage points, while a poll of about 1,000 people a wave was far closer. For that estimate, the giant survey was worth less than a random sample of 10 people.
core_insight: Estimation error = data quality (the correlation between who responds and the answer) x a data-quantity term x problem difficulty. In a large population even a tiny selection bias swamps sample size: more biased data just gives a more confident wrong answer.
key_visual: A population of millions as a fine mosaic. A random scoop of 1,000 tiles gives a histogram centered on the truth with a modest error bar. A huge self-selected scoop, where tiles are slightly more likely to be picked if vaccinated, gives a razor-thin error bar centered in the wrong place. Meng's three-factor equation assembles on screen, with the 'data defect correlation' highlighted as the knob that matters.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: more responses means more accuracy; confidence intervals shrink as n grows. Simulate a tiny self-selection bias (rho = 0.005) in a population of 250 million; the error refuses to shrink. Fix attempts: demographic weighting helps only if those variables explain who responds. Benchmark against a probability sample; the real fix is the design.
real_world_anchor: Bradley et al. (2021), 'Unrepresentative Big Surveys Significantly Overestimated US Vaccine Uptake', Nature (Delphi-Facebook and Census Household Pulse versus Axios-Ipsos, benchmarked to CDC data); Xiao-Li Meng (2018), 'Statistical Paradises and Paradoxes in Big Data (I)', Annals of Applied Statistics. Historical echo: the 1936 Literary Digest poll, with about 2.4 million returns, predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: 'Fewer than 10' is Bradley et al.'s bias-adjusted effective sample size for the vaccination-rate estimate in April 2021, not a verdict on the surveys' usefulness for other questions. The Literary Digest failure is now attributed largely to nonresponse bias as well as its sampling frame (Squire, 1988).

title: A Poll Can Match the Census and Still Be Wrong
hook: When Pew ran a phone survey with a 9% response rate, it matched government benchmarks on most demographics, yet 55% of respondents said they had volunteered in the past year, versus 27% in a high-response government survey.
core_insight: Weighting fixes imbalance only on the variables you weight by; if the reason people respond is related to the outcome (civic engagement, education, partisanship), demographic weighting leaves the bias in place.
key_visual: Respondents as tiles with visible attributes (age, sex) and a hidden one (civic-mindedness).
