Weighting is shown as tiles inflating and deflating until the age and sex bars match census targets perfectly, while the hidden-trait bar stays skewed. Then raking on education is added: a new set of bars snaps into place and the estimate moves.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: report the raw poll. Iterate: weight by age and sex; demographics match, volunteering is still far off. Add education weighting; estimates correlated with education improve. Show the 2016 U.S. case, where many state polls did not weight by education. What remains is bias from unobserved drivers of response.
real_world_anchor: Pew Research Center (2012), 'Assessing the Representativeness of Public Opinion Surveys': typical telephone response rates fell from 36% in 1997 to 9% in 2012; 55% of respondents reported volunteering versus 27% in the Current Population Survey supplement. AAPOR (2017), 'An Evaluation of 2016 Election Polls in the U.S.', identified lack of education weighting as one source of error in state polls.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Low response rates do not automatically mean bias; Pew found many measures were accurate, and bias arises when responding correlates with the outcome. National polls in 2016 were fairly accurate; the larger errors were in some key state polls.

title: How a Poll of Gamers Forecast a Presidential Election
hook: In 2012, a poll run on the Xbox gaming platform drew respondents who were 93% male, versus 47% of voters. After statistical adjustment, its estimates were in line with forecasts from leading poll aggregators.
core_insight: Multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP): model opinion as a function of demographics, borrowing strength across similar cells (partial pooling), then reweight the predictions to the population's known composition, turning a skewed sample into a usable estimate when selection is explained by the modeled variables.
key_visual: A large grid of demographic cells (age x sex x race x education x state x party) drawn as tiles. Raw Xbox respondents pile up in the young-male tiles while most others stay nearly empty. The model fills sparse tiles with estimates pulled toward similar tiles (shrinkage arrows). Finally each tile is resized to its share of the electorate and combined into a forecast line tracking the campaign.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: the raw Xbox numbers, heavily skewed toward Romney. Naive weighting cell by cell: empty and tiny cells make estimates explode. Fix: a multilevel model with partial pooling across cells (Stein-style shrinkage), followed by poststratification. Validate against the actual result and exit polls.
real_world_anchor: Wang, Rothschild, Goel & Gelman (2015), 'Forecasting Elections with Non-Representative Polls', International Journal of Forecasting: the 2012 Xbox sample was 93% male (versus 47% of voters) and 65% aged 18-29 (versus 19%); MRP was introduced by Gelman & Little (1997).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: MRP corrects only for selection explained by variables in the model; it is not magic for any convenience sample. Wang et al. also poststratified on party identification and past vote, which mattered; mention it.

title: How Google's Flu Detector Lost to Weeks-Old Data
hook: Google Flu Trends promised real-time flu tracking from search queries. In early 2013 it estimated more than double the CDC's flu levels, and, as critics pointed out, simply projecting forward from CDC data a couple of weeks old would have done better.
core_insight: Big-data predictors built on correlations can latch onto seasonal coincidences and break when user behavior or the platform changes; combining big data with small, well-measured data beats either alone.
key_visual: Two time series race week by week: CDC flu levels in white and GFT estimates in orange. Early on they overlap; later GFT drifts above and overshoots the 2012-13 peak by about a factor of two. Behind the scenes, roughly 50 million candidate search queries rain down as particles and a filter keeps 45, some flagged red as merely winter-correlated. A third line, a model using lagged CDC data, hugs the truth.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: pick the search terms most correlated with past flu data; winter-seasonal terms sneak in. Fail: the model largely missed the out-of-season 2009 H1N1 pandemic and later overshot as search behavior and Google's own search features changed. Fix: combine search signals with lagged CDC data and recalibrate continually.
real_world_anchor: Ginsberg et al. (2009), 'Detecting Influenza Epidemics Using Search Engine Query Data', Nature (about 50 million queries screened, 45 selected); Lazer, Kennedy, King & Vespignani (2014), 'The Parable of Google Flu: Traps in Big Data Analysis', Science: GFT overestimated flu prevalence in 100 of 108 weeks starting in August 2011.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: GFT was not worthless: Lazer et al. showed that combining GFT with lagged CDC data outperformed either alone. The 'weeks-old CDC data' comparison comes from Lazer's commentary on the paper; the formal finding is the combination result.

title: The Strange Bump at 20 Friends
hook: Facebook's friend-count distribution, measured in 2011, has a kink near 20 friends and a hard cutoff at 5,000. Neither is a law of human sociality: both were put there by the platform itself.
core_insight: Digital trace data are jointly produced by people and by the platform's algorithms, defaults and user population, so patterns in platform data can reflect engineering decisions ('algorithmic confounding') as much as human behavior.
key_visual: A smooth, heavy-tailed degree distribution draws itself; then a nudging hand pushes users with fewer than 20 friends to add more, and a bump forms at 20. A wall slams down at 5,000. A second layer: a 'people you may know' engine adds triangle-closing edges in gold, inflating the network's clustering, so its 'social' statistics now partly measure the code.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: fit a theory of human friendship to the raw degree distribution and 'explain' the kink. Iterate: overlay product features on the data; simulate a recommender that closes triangles and show it alone raises transitivity. Fix: treat the platform as part of the data-generating process; seek documentation, natural experiments or cross-platform comparisons.
real_world_anchor: Ugander, Karrer, Backstrom & Marlow (2011), 'The Anatomy of the Facebook Social Graph' (arXiv): the kink near 20 friends is attributed to product features encouraging low-friend-count users to add friends, and the cutoff to Facebook's 5,000-friend limit; 'algorithmic confounding' as discussed in Matthew Salganik, Bit by Bit (2018).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The kink is a modest feature, not a giant spike; draw it to scale. Algorithmic confounding is distinct from population bias (who uses the platform at all); both matter, so name them separately.

title: Three Facts That Can Identify You
hook: Your ZIP code, birth date and sex sound anonymous. Using 1990 census data, that combination was estimated to single out about 87% of Americans, and it was used to find a governor's 'anonymized' medical records.
core_insight: Removing names is not anonymization: combinations of ordinary attributes (quasi-identifiers) are often unique, so 'anonymous' datasets can be linked to public ones and re-identified.
key_visual: A crowd of 10,000 person icons. Filter by ZIP code: thousands remain. Add sex: half. Add birth year: dozens. Add full birth date: one icon glows alone. Then a linkage animation: an 'anonymous' medical table and a public voter roll slide together and matching rows snap into named records. A final scene: four points on a grid-map are enough to isolate one movement trace among many.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: strip names and ID numbers and release. Attack: join with a voter list on ZIP + birth date + sex; re-identified. Fix attempt: coarsen birth date to year; uniqueness drops, but rich data such as location traces remain unique. This sets up k-anonymity (next) and differential privacy.
real_world_anchor: Latanya Sweeney (2000), 'Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely', Carnegie Mellon Data Privacy Working Paper 3 (the 87% estimate), and her 1997 re-identification of Massachusetts Governor William Weld's hospital records; de Montjoye et al. (2013), 'Unique in the Crowd: The Privacy Bounds of Human Mobility', Scientific Reports: four spatio-temporal points uniquely identified 95% of 1.5 million mobile-phone users.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Golle (2006) re-estimated about 63% uniqueness using 2000 census data; present 87% as an estimate tied to its data year. Keep the explanation conceptual; do not demonstrate re-identifying real, living people.

title: Hiding in a Crowd Isn't Enough
hook: One fix for re-identification is to make every person in a released table look identical to at least k - 1 others. But if all k people in a group share the same diagnosis, the secret is out anyway.
core_insight: k-anonymity protects against identity linkage, not attribute disclosure: homogeneous groups and background knowledge leak sensitive values, and in high-dimensional data achieving k-anonymity destroys most of the data's usefulness.
key_visual: A table of records as rows of colored cells. Generalization squeezes values into ranges (age 34 becomes 30-39, a ZIP code loses its last digits) and rows merge into blocks of at least k. An 'attacker' knows which block a neighbor is in; if that block's diagnosis column is uniformly red, the secret is revealed. The next fix (l-diversity) recolors blocks to be mixed, and a skewed-distribution attack still shifts beliefs.
build_fail_iterate: Build: k-anonymize a toy medical table; homogeneity attack. Fix: l-diversity; skewness and similarity attacks. Fix: t-closeness; usefulness collapses. Fail in high dimensions: with many attributes nearly every record must be suppressed or generalized away. The escalating arms race motivates a different approach: differential privacy.
real_world_anchor: Latanya Sweeney (2002), 'k-Anonymity: A Model for Protecting Privacy', International Journal of Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-Based Systems; Machanavajjhala et al. (2007), 'l-Diversity: Privacy Beyond k-Anonymity', ACM TKDD; Li, Li & Venkatasubramanian (2007) on t-closeness; Charu Aggarwal (2005), 'On k-Anonymity and the Curse of Dimensionality', VLDB.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: k-anonymity is a meaningful but limited guarantee, not useless. Each successive definition patched a specific attack; present them as historical refinements rather than a single failure.

title: The Privacy Trick That Starts With a Coin Flip
hook: To learn how many people cheated on their taxes without anyone being able to prove a single person did, have each flip a coin in secret: heads, answer truthfully; tails, flip again and answer 'yes' for heads, 'no' for tails. Every individual answer is deniable, yet the true rate can be recovered.
core_insight: Differential privacy guarantees that any one person's data barely changes what is published (bounded by a privacy budget epsilon), achieved by adding calibrated randomness; it trades accuracy for protection that holds whatever an attacker already knows.
key_visual: A crowd answers via animated coin flips, so the 'yes' tiles are a mix of truthful and coin-forced answers. The observed yes-rate is unwound algebraically to the true rate (true = 2 x observed - 0.5), with error bars. Then the formal picture: two neighboring datasets, identical except for one person, produce two overlapping noise distributions (Laplace curves) whose ratio is bounded by e^epsilon. A slider raises epsilon: the curves separate, accuracy rises and privacy falls.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: release exact counts for small groups; a differencing attack (count with and without one person) reveals individuals. Fix 1: round or suppress small cells; still vulnerable to combining many published statistics (database reconstruction). Fix 2: add Laplace noise scaled to sensitivity/epsilon and track the total privacy budget across all releases. Plot the accuracy-privacy trade-off curve.
real_world_anchor: Stanley Warner (1965), 'Randomized Response: A Survey Technique for Eliminating Evasive Answer Bias', JASA; Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith (2006), 'Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis'; Dinur & Nissim (2003) on reconstructing data from too many accurate statistics; the U.S. Census Bureau adopted differential privacy for its 2020 Census data products.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Differential privacy protects whether any individual's data were included; it does not prevent population-level inferences (a study can still show smoking causes cancer). The Census implementation was contested, with concerns about accuracy for small areas; present the debate fairly. This two-coin randomized response satisfies epsilon = ln 3.

title: 'It's Public Data' Isn't an Ethical Argument
hook: In 2008, researchers released a de-identified dataset of Facebook profiles from an unnamed university's students. Others worked out which university it was within days, and some of the profile data had been visible only to members of that campus network.
core_insight: Accessibility is not consent. Privacy depends on context: information shared under one set of norms (friends, a campus network) can cause harm when moved into another (a research dataset, a public release), so ethical data collection weighs expectations, harms and re-identification risk, not just technical access.
key_visual: Information as glowing packets flowing between labeled circles (contexts): 'friends', 'campus network', 'researchers', 'the world', each with its own norm color. A scraper vacuum pulls packets out of the campus circle into a 'public dataset' circle, where their colors clash with the new context. Then a re-identification beam sweeps across the 'anonymous' dataset and lights up its source.
build_fail_iterate: Naive protocol: 'If it is accessible, collect it; remove names; release.' Walk through each failure: hidden visibility settings, re-identification from distinctive attributes, terms of service, and harm to people who never consented. Iterate toward a better protocol: a contextual-integrity check, data minimization, aggregation, controlled access and ethics review.
real_world_anchor: Michael Zimmer (2010), 'But the Data Is Already Public: On the Ethics of Research in Facebook', Ethics and Information Technology, on the 'Tastes, Ties, and Time' dataset; Helen Nissenbaum (2004), 'Privacy as Contextual Integrity', Washington Law Review; Fiesler & Proferes (2018), 'Participant Perceptions of Twitter Research Ethics', Social Media + Society, finding many users unaware that public tweets are used in research.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Do not name or depict any individuals from the dataset. The original researchers took steps to protect privacy; the case shows how hard anonymization is, not malicious intent. Legality (terms of service, law) and ethics are different questions and vary by jurisdiction.

title: The Tiny-Effect Experiment That Sparked a Huge Backlash
hook: In 2012, Facebook altered the News Feeds of about 689,000 users for a week to show fewer positive or fewer negative posts. The measured effects on what people later posted were tiny, yet the study set off a global debate about consent.
core_insight: Online platforms experiment on users constantly; publishing this study forced the question of informed consent. Research-ethics principles (respect for persons, beneficence, justice) apply even when effects are small and terms of service technically permit it, and huge samples make minuscule effects 'statistically significant'.
key_visual: A News Feed as a vertical stream of colored post cards (yellow positive, blue negative). A filter silently removes a fraction of yellow cards for one group and blue cards for another. Users' later posts are counted as tiny bars; the difference has to be magnified 1,000x to be visible, beside a Cohen's d ruler reading roughly 0.001 to 0.02. Then a balance scale weighs 'minimal risk' against 'no informed consent, no opt-out'.
build_fail_iterate: Naive logic: 'Platforms A/B test all the time, users agreed to the terms, and the effect was tiny, so there is no issue.' Test each premise against the Belmont principles: consent (a data-use policy versus informed consent), risk (unknown in advance), possibly vulnerable users, and independent review. Iterate toward modern practice: ethics review for platform research, transparency and opt-outs.
real_world_anchor: Kramer, Guillory & Hancock (2014), 'Experimental Evidence of Massive-Scale Emotional Contagion through Social Networks', PNAS (689,003 users over one week in January 2012; effect sizes as small as d = 0.001); PNAS Editorial Expression of Concern (Verma, 2014); The Belmont Report (1979).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Report the effects accurately: the changes in posted words were statistically significant but very small, and the study measured posts, not felt emotions. Cornell's IRB concluded its researchers were not directly engaged in human-subjects research because they analyzed results provided by Facebook; state this rather than claiming no review occurred.

title: How a Policing Algorithm Can Confirm Its Own Predictions
hook: Send patrols where past records show more crime and you will record more crime there, because that is where officers are looking. In simulation, a predictive-policing algorithm can keep concentrating on the same neighborhoods even when true crime is spread evenly.
core_insight: When a model's predictions decide which data get collected, it forms a feedback loop: observed outcomes reflect the model's own choices, so early errors and biases are amplified rather than corrected, a Polya-urn dynamic.
key_visual: A city of two districts with identical true crime, shown as an equal rain of red sparks. Patrol cars are allocated by past recorded counts, and only sparks inside a patrol's view become recorded tallies. The district with an early lead gets more patrols, records more, and gets more patrols still: the Polya urn of episode 80 visibly running. A corrected version weights observations by detection probability, and allocations converge to equal.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: allocate patrols in proportion to recorded crime and simulate; runaway concentration. Fix 1: add random exploration; it slows the loop but does not remove the bias in the records. Fix 2: correct for differential observation (count only incidents discovered independently of patrol allocation, or reweight by detection probability). Remaining limit: reported-crime data carry their own social biases.
real_world_anchor: Lum & Isaac (2016), 'To Predict and Serve?', Significance: applying a predictive-policing algorithm to Oakland drug-crime records concentrated predictions in largely Black and low-income neighborhoods, while public-health survey estimates suggested drug use was spread across the city; Ensign et al. (2018), 'Runaway Feedback Loops in Predictive Policing', Proceedings of FAT* (a Polya urn model).
pitfalls_for_accuracy: Lum and Isaac's result is a demonstration using historical records, not an audit of a deployed system. Do not claim all predictive policing behaves this way; the loop arises when incidents discovered by patrols drive future allocation.

title: Why No Algorithm Can Be Fair in Every Way at Once
hook: A criminal risk score can be calibrated for two groups, so that 'high risk' means the same reoffense rate in both, and still flag people who never reoffend in one group at nearly twice the rate of the other. When base rates differ, both cannot be fixed at once.
core_insight: When groups have different base rates, no imperfect classifier can be calibrated within each group and also have equal false-positive and false-negative rates across groups; choosing a fairness criterion is a value judgment, not a technical detail.
key_visual: Two populations as dot grids with different base rates (more red dots in group B). One shared, calibrated score slides a threshold across both. Four live meters per group (calibration, false-positive rate, false-negative rate, positive predictive value): adjusting thresholds to equalize false-positive rates knocks calibration out; restoring calibration splits the false-positive rates again. The constraints are drawn as planes whose only common point is 'perfect prediction' or 'equal base rates'.
build_fail_iterate: Naive: 'just remove the race variable'; proxies such as neighborhood and prior arrests carry the information and disparities persist. Fix attempt: equalize false-positive rates with group-specific thresholds; calibration breaks. Fix attempt: calibrate; unequal error rates return. Conclusion: decide, with the people affected, which errors matter most and why; the math only exposes the trade-off.
real_world_anchor: Angwin, Larson, Mattu & Kirchner (2016), 'Machine Bias', ProPublica: in Broward County, Black defendants who did not reoffend were labeled higher risk by COMPAS at nearly twice the rate of white defendants (about 45% vs 23%); Northpointe's response emphasized calibration; Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan (2016; ITCS 2017) and Chouldechova (2017), Big Data, proved the incompatibility.
pitfalls_for_accuracy: The theorem's only escapes are equal base rates or perfect prediction. ProPublica's and Northpointe's analyses were each mathematically correct about different metrics; do not frame one side as simply wrong. Base-rate differences in recorded rearrests may themselves reflect biased measurement.
